utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please be seated. Good morning, everybody. Registrar, may I ask you to call the case on the Appeals Chamber's agenda.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-95-13/1-R.1, the Prosecutor versus Veselin Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask Mr. Sljivancanin if he can hear me and follow the proceedings through the translation. Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to all in the courtroom. Yes, I can follow the proceedings and I can understand what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Helen Brady appearing together with Mr. Paul Rogers on behalf of the Prosecution, and together with us today Mr. Kyle Wood and our case manager Mr. Colin Nawrot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Brady. This is a hearing held as part of a pre-review proceeding in the case of Prosecutor versus Veselin Sljivancanin. At the outset, I will briefly summarise the issues which are pending before the Appeals Chamber and the manner in which we will proceed today. I will underscore again that none of my comments today expresses in any way the Appeals Chamber's views on any aspect of the review motion. This hearing addresses two issues: First, the evidentiary value and the relevance of Mr. Panic's anticipated testimony regarding certain issues relating to Mr. Sljivancanin's conviction for aiding and abetting murder as a violation of the laws or customs of war; and second, whether this anticipated testimony could potentially constitute a new fact within the scope of Rules 119 and 120 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. During this hearing, counsel will first examine the witness, Miodrag Panic, and present summary arguments concerning his testimony. They will then present submissions on whether Mr. Panic's further evidence constitutes a new fact. I would underscore -- I will underscore that parties should provide precise references to materials supporting their arguments. I would also underscore that every time parties refer to a new document, they should provide the document number they assigned it when providing copies to the Chamber. Before turning to this morning's proceedings, I would like to apologise, I did not call on the counsel, the counsel for Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. On behalf of Defence of Mr. Sljivancanin, my name is Novak Lukic, I am lead counsel for Mr. Sljivancanin. Here with me is Mr. Stephane Bourgon as a co-counsel. There are two legal assistants, Ms. Maja Dokmanovic and Mrs. Caroline Bouchard-Lauzon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. And I apologise for not calling on you earlier. I will now turn to the timetable for this morning's proceedings. This hearing will proceed according to the schedule outlined in the order responding to the Prosecutor's motion on hearing management and the revised Scheduling Order issued on 21 May 2010. Counsel for Mr. Sljivancanin will conduct the examination-in-chief of Mr. Panic for one hour, 15 minutes. Following a 15-minute pause, the Prosecution will then cross-examine Mr. Panic for one hour, 15 minutes. After a 15-minute pause, counsel for Mr. Sljivancanin will conduct a re-examination of Mr. Panic for 15 minutes, followed by 15 minutes of summary arguments concerning Mr. Panic's testimony. Finally, the Prosecution will present summary arguments concerning Mr. Panic's testimony for 15 minutes. I note that the Chamber will look favourably on any request by counsel for Mr. Sljivancanin to re-allocate some of their time from examination-in-chief to re-examination. In the afternoon at 1.45 p.m., counsel for Mr. Sljivancanin will present submissions on whether Mr. Panic's testimony is a new fact for 45 minutes. This will be followed by submissions from the Prosecution on the same issue for 45 minutes and a reply by counsel for Mr. Sljivancanin for 15 minutes. Of course, parties need not exhaust the entirety of their allotted time. It will be most helpful to the Appeals Chamber if the parties could present their submissions in a precise and clear manner. I wish to remind the parties that the Judges may interrupt them at any time to ask questions or they may prefer to ask questions following each party's submissions. I would also remind parties that certain exhibits are under seal; therefore, if the parties wish to refer to these documents, they should request private session. Having said this, I would now call -- like to call Witness Miodrag Panic. The Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Panic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, could you please read the solemn declaration given to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Panic. You may now be seated. Mr. Panic, you -- Mr. Panic, you will be asked to testify in conjunction with Mr. Sljivancanin's application for review of his conviction for aiding and abetting murder as a violation of the laws or customs of war. In the course of the morning, counsel for Mr. Sljivancanin and for the Prosecution will both put questions to you concerning certain issues relating to this conviction. Judges may also choose to ask questions. I would now like to invite counsel for Mr. Sljivancanin to begin with his examination-in-chief, for which you have, as you know, one hour and 15 minutes starting from now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Judges from the Appeals Chamber. Good morning to my colleagues from the Prosecution. I will be conducting the examination-in-chief of Witness Panic this morning, and for this purpose I would like to have the usher give to the witness a binder, which includes all the documents that has been given to the Appeals Chamber, simply to make things easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. This binder was shown to the Prosecution this morning, and it includes nothing more than the documents that we intend maybe to use. Mr. President, if I may add before I begin, you have suggested the possibility of re-allocating some of our examination-in-chief time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Registry, would you give us one more set? We have only four sets. Oh, you have one. We're all right. Sorry. I'm terribly sorry, Mr. Bourgon. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I apologise. You indicated earlier, Mr. President, the possibility of re-allocating some of our examination-in-chief time to re-examination. I will see if that will be necessary. I hope, Mr. President, to complete my examination-in-chief within one hour, but of course we never know how these things go.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, General Panic.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, we have met this week, but allow me to introduce myself for the record. My name is Stephane Bourgon and I am accompanied this morning for your testimony by Mr. Novak Lukic, by Ms. Maja Dokmanovic, and by Ms. Caroline Bouchard-Lauzon. General, I will be asking you a series of questions this morning. I would like to remind you that at any time, should there be any question that you do not understand, please do not hesitate to interrupt me so that I can say the questions over again. It is very important that you understand each question that I will put to you. General, when we met yesterday, I explained to you the purpose of the hearing this morning, so we will go straight to the essence of your testimony. However, before I do so, I would like to point out that the -- even though the Judges from the Appeals Chamber are most likely familiar with your testimony in the Sljivancanin case when it was at trial, it is the first time that they see you this morning. So for the benefit of the Judges, can you briefly summarise your military career.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: I graduated from the military academy in 1972, when I became a professional officer of the Yugoslav People's Army. During my professional career, I held all command positions that exist, from platoon commander to commander of the corps of the special units, assistant Chief of General Staff for land forces, and I ended my career as head of the inspectorate for combat-readiness in 2002, when I retired with the rank of lieutenant-general. During my education and military service, I completed all military schools that existed, including the school of national defence. I'm a retiree now and I live in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I will be asking my questions to you this morning based on the series of topic, and my first topic this morning is your testimony in the Mrksic, Sljivancanin, and Radic case. Do you recall, General, when you testified before this Tribunal in this case?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall. It was in 2006, in the first half of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, did you have an opportunity to review your testimony since then?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: When was that and how did you do that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: I reviewed it about a month ago, and this is how I did it: I received from Mr. Lukic's office, through Ms. Dokmanovic, the video recording of that testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what language was this recording in?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: That video recording was in my mother tongue, in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, having watched your testimony, are there any of your answers that you gave at the time that you would like to modify today?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: When I reviewed that testimony of mine, I decided that I stand by what I said then when I testified, except that now I could clarify certain events and certain minute details related to that testimony. Perhaps I could clarify certain events with greater precision.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, General, is there any one issue that comes to your mind this morning that you could perhaps provide further clarification on?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Well, now, after everything, I could explain with greater precision the place and role of Mr. Sljivancanin during the evacuation of the hospital; more specifically, his role in the field of security -- or rather, the security-related selection of paramilitary formations that had sought shelter in the hospital. I could explain that part in greater detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I will not be asking any questions about this topic today. Maybe the Prosecution will in cross-examination, but that's a different matter. I move to my next topic, which is the judgement that was rendered in the trial of Mrksic, Sljivancanin, and Radic. Sir, do you know when the trial judgement was rendered in that case?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: That judgement was rendered in 2007, sometime in the month of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Were you interested in the outcome of this trial; and if so, why?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was and our entire public was very interested in that. I in particular, because I know the man concerned. I was with them when certain things happened and this was in particular due to the fact that I testified before this court as well. That is why I was interested in the outcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, moving on to my next topic, which is the outcome of the judgement. Do you recall what happened to Mr. Radic in that case and what was your reaction?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recall. Mr. Radic was acquitted of all the charges. I found that acceptable. I was very pleased. I had never even known of Radic. I did not realise, as I said here when I testified, how come he became part of all of that. So I'm glad that that is how things turned out for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what about Sljivancanin, do you know what happened to him and what was your reaction after the first-degree judgement?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. Mr. Sljivancanin was sentenced to five years in prison. That is a serious sentence, but my understanding was that that was the price to be paid for where he was during the Vukovar operation and the fact that he personally was more exposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you elaborate on what you mean by "he ... was more exposed"?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Sljivancanin, as you can see him here, he's a striking person. He has personal courage. He was in many places. He was in many places where things happened, and in particular towards the end of the operations, he was in the places where civilians were supposed to be protected physically; that is to say, those who had been taken prisoner and those who were frail. I believe that this is a personal shortcoming of his, that he liked to have his picture taken, he liked being exposed in the media. For the public, he was a media personality. That's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about Mrksic, what happened to him and what was your reaction to that judgement?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic, as the commander, was sentenced to 20 years. That is a long sentence. It's serious punishment, and I took it to be the price of the -- for the fact that he was the commander. Being commander involves responsibility and glory. At that point in time, it was my understanding that that was the price to be paid for command responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I move to my next topic, which is the reason why Mrksic was convicted. Did you come to learn, Mr. Panic, as to why Mrksic was convicted?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: I learned that Mrksic was convicted because he had ordered the withdrawal of the security detail from Ovcara, where the prisoner had been guarded.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And was this a surprise to you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: This was a major surprise for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Why so?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: I know Mrksic as commander pretty well. We worked together for a number of years. I know that he is a stern but fair commander. I could not believe that that was possible, that it was possible for him to have ordered that, approved of that, or agreed with that kind of decision, to withdraw the security detail. When I think about this, he never communicated that to anyone. So that was my surprise first of all. How come he was being convicted for something that we had not known about at all? And again, as I think about this, he's the only one who could have made that kind of decision as commander. It is only the commander who can make that kind of decision, but I had never known of that decision nor can I believe that and I cannot even be convinced now that he had done something like that. That was a major surprise to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let us move to the appeals judgement or the second-degree judgement. Did you come to learn, Mr. Panic, that the judgement was under appeal?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did know. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And how did you come to learn this?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Well, it was in the media and our public was greatly interested in that, so was I and all my comrades too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you remember the date of the Appeals Chamber or the second-degree judgement?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. I remember that Mr. Sljivancanin was on provisional release then, and he had to go back because the judgement was supposed to be rendered. And that was in December -- sorry, no, that was in May, about a year ago -- or actually to be more specific, while I was preparing a bit here, I saw that it was in May 2009, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. What about the outcome of the second-degree judgement, do you recall first of all what happened to Mrksic and what was your reaction to that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know that Mrksic's sentence of 20 years in prison was confirmed, and I had expected that, in view of the fact that he had been commander and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what about Sljivancanin, what happened to him in this second-degree judgement and what -- how did the people react in Belgrade to this?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as Mr. Sljivancanin's judgement was concerned, for me this was a major shock, a major surprise, first of all for me personally and also for the public in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now tell us, sir, why was this a major shock for you personally?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: For me personally this was a major shock. All of a sudden he got 12 years additionally. We thought that he had served his sentence and that he was coming back and that he would be free. However, he got a sentence that was more than three times higher. This is what he got at this new trial. Then I was greatly surprised when I saw why it was that he was given this sentence. That is what surprised me in particular. I understand that it is for the Court to assess all the facts and to compare them. However, at that point in time I did not see that Sljivancanin had deserved that kind of punishment for what was stated there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, can you explain how this took place exactly. How did you come to be shocked and when did that happen?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, I followed the proceedings on the internet. So I was watching and I couldn't believe my eyes and ears. I was watching, reading, and it seemed less than normal to me, uncomprehensible, one sentence or two sentences, namely, that Mr. Sljivancanin was -- got that sentence because Mrksic as commander had ordered to withdraw the security detail from Ovcara. If he had communicated that -- or rather, that he communicated that to Sljivancanin and that he, as a security organ, failed to protect the prisoners at Ovcara -- or rather, it says there that he didn't exert influence on Mrksic to change his decision. After that, I tried to see in the media whether that was really so, whether it may have been a translation error or maybe I misheard. Many people called me on that day and I spoke to many people, but things remained as I had understood them in the first place. I couldn't wait for my daughter to come back from work on that afternoon. She speaks excellent English because she studied at Cambridge, she got her doctoral degree there. I wanted to consult her and see whether she could translate to me from English and check whether I had understood things correctly. And he really -- was able to find a summary that states the same thing. If I can repeat -- or I don't know if I should repeat what it said there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, General, did your daughter and yourself find such information; and if so, where?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes. My daughter was able to do so. It's an English version, a summary in the English language, which she translated to me. It was on the internet.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what was this the summary of?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: It was a summary of the sentence, the judgement of the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, can you look in the binder that is in front of you at tab number 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: For the Appeals Chamber, Mr. President, this is Exhibit RD8.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Yes, this is the summary of the judgement of the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Is there any specific part of this document that was most important for you on that day; and if so, can you identify that for us, please.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes. All of this was important to me. I read that all. But what shocked me especially and which made me react as a human being is this part, the summary. The Trial Chamber notes that the -- sorry, the Appeals Chamber notes that the Trial Chamber -- et cetera --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, can you tell us where you are in the document, please, what page, so that everybody can follow in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Well, as I turn the pages, I'm looking at the typed pages, page 2, page 3, 4, 5, and then we reach the sixth typed page.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, the document you have before you is in what language, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: It's in my language, the Serbian language, and it's the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And is this the exact document that you saw that night?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In that language?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: It was in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. Tell us -- please proceed to tell us what is the paragraph that was most important to you.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: To me this paragraph was the most important, the second paragraph on page 6. It says here: "However, the only reasonable conclusion that can be drawn is that Mr. Mrksic, during their meeting after the return of Mr. Sljivancanin to Negoslavci on that night, said to Mr. Sljivancanin that he had withdrawn the members of the JNA who were protecting the prisoners of war at Ovcara."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, sir, tell us why this paragraph was suddenly so important to you.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: This became important to me -- I testified here and I testified to a series of facts, but this is completely new to me. That is why it attracted my attention, because I know that I was at Negoslavci at the time. I know that I was at the command post. I know when Mr. Sljivancanin arrived. I know that he met Mr. Mrksic. And I know that Mrksic then didn't say to him that he had withdrawn the security detail. That is why this was a surprise to me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to by reference to the English text direct us exactly to the paragraph that [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will, Mr. President. I'm looking for the paragraph right now and it is on the sixth page, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if it helps, it's on the sixth page of the English under Prosecution Appeal, it's the third paragraph, and it's in the middle of the third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: "The Appeals Chamber notes ..." that's how it starts; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, Mr. President. I just found. Thank you to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So, sir, having seen this information on that summary, how did you react to this?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Having seen this, I was upset. I couldn't sleep that night and I could hardly wait for dawn to call up Mr. Lukic's office, which I did first thing in the morning. And I was able to reach Mr. Lukic's office. He wasn't there at the time. I suppose that he was here -- or rather, he certainly was. Ms. Dokmanovic answered the phone. I asked whether I could establish contact in any way with Attorney Lukic. She said she would do all she could when she gets the chance to have Mr. Lukic call me. And in the evening hours of the same day, Mr. Lukic contacted me from The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when Mr. Lukic called you, can you tell us what you told him?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: When he called me, I [as interpreted] immediately asked me, without beating about the bush, what happened, Mr. Lukic? Where did this sudden turn come from? Is this possible? Is it true that Mr. Sljivancanin was convicted because Mr. Mrksic gave him the information that he had withdrawn the security detail and Mr. Sljivancanin failed to try to make him change his decision, as it says? Mr. Lukic said to me, "Yes, indeed, this is true."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Go on -- please go on. Explain what happened during that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: I said to him, "Mr. Lukic, that's wrong. I was there. I was present during the conversation. It's impossible that Mrksic gave that information to Sljivancanin without giving it to me, who was there, or before that or at any time. That is simply wrong. And I really ask you that we do something." Well, this is a brief version.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what did Mr. Lukic say in response to this?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic said, "Keep this information. When I come to Belgrade, we'll speak about it some more, and you try to remember everything that happened that evening at the command post, try to remember who else was present who could corroborate that."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And did -- Mr. Lukic did travel to Belgrade to see you; and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic arrived in Belgrade a few days later and we spoke about this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened during that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic informed me of his arrival and we met at his office. We then spoke some more about the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did Mr. Lukic tell you anything about the information you provided him with?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Well, we talked about it. I again asked him whether everything was really like that, and he gave me a more detailed explanation. Then we spoke about the information I had given to him. Mr. Lukic was then interested to hear why I was reacting and what kind of information I could relate to him, what kind of facts I could speak about. He asked me whether I was present at the command post, who else was there, what they spoke about, when Mr. Sljivancanin arrived at the command post, what Mr. Mrksic and Mr. Sljivancanin spoke about. He asked me why I hadn't disclosed that information to anybody earlier, why I was -- contacted him about it now. And I simply said that I had testified on several occasions, I had given many statements, but nobody had ever asked me about it. He also asked me whether I -- if a new testimony should become necessary, whether I would be willing to testify, and I said, "Yes, certainly, any time."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me move to --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: If I may. He merely said that I should keep it to myself, this information, and then we would see after a certain time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, maybe that brings another question from me. Did you sign a statement on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, at that time was this -- how much was this reported in the media in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: This was present in the media. They wrote a lot about the judgement, but there was also a small article in the media about the Sljivancanin Defence having received some new information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, if you can turn at tab 14 in the binder in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And for the Appeals Chamber, this is Exhibit RD14, 1-4. There is an unofficial translation in English, Mr. President, but the original is in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you tell us if you were -- if you came to learn this information at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw this in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, it says here in the middle of the document -- now, of course I have the English version. It says: "New information which we have received and which we have already started to investigate ..." Does that correspond in any way to the information you provided Mr. Lukic with?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This matches. I saw this. I -- concluding that from reading between the lines that this was the information that originated from me -- well, maybe somebody else too, but I certainly recognised myself in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let me move then to our next topic, which is whether you had any other meetings following this first meeting with members of the Sljivancanin Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: It was a few months later in Belgrade. I met you, Mr. Lukic, and there was also Ms. Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: How long did this meeting last and what was discussed then?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: It was a short meeting. It didn't last long. I understood that it was all about meeting each other and my corroborating the information I had, and I learned then that I might be called to testify and you asked me whether I would be willing to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you provide a statement on this occasion, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, it's a known fact in these proceedings that you did provide a statement; when was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: I'm happy for my learned friend to lead the date if he wants to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So the statement that we have on record is dated 8th October of 2009. Can you recall when and how you came about to provide this statement?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the exact date of that statement. I wrote it by hand on two pages, and I did so in the presence of Mr. Lukic at his office. There were other people around, but they were doing their own work. They were in their respective offices and I met Mr. Lukic in private.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And were you provided with any guide-lines as to what to put in that statement?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: I got brief guide-lines like bullet points. Apart from stating my personal information, what I was and where I was, I was also instructed to write down what I had heard, that is, the contents of the conversation between Mrksic and Sljivancanin. Firstly, whether it was correct that Mrksic had told Sljivancanin that he had withdrawn the security detail, and Mr. Sljivancanin failing to try to make him change his decision. Then stating the reason why I was volunteering this information only then. And finally, why I had decided to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So tell us, physically how did you provide this statement to Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Let me just add, Lukic suggested to me to add another sentence, whether or not I sought protective measures, and I stated that I was willing to testify without any protective measures. I signed the statement with my own hand and handed it to Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, sir, between the time that you provided this statement in October of 2009 and today, did you have any other meetings with members of the Sljivancanin Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes. I met Ms. Dokmanovic in Belgrade and I also had a meeting with the Defence team, that is, you and Mr. Lukic, when I came here to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I see that time is running out, General, so I'm going to move straight to a different topic, and that is concerning the people that you met before you testified in the first-degree judgement, first-degree trial. I'd like you to recap very quickly all the people you spoke to before your first testimony in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, that does appear to be a rather broad question --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: It doesn't appear to be focused on any particular issue. I expect he had a conversation with a lot of people over a -- about a lot of things, but perhaps my learned friend wants to try to be a little bit more precise about what it was he spoke to and which people he spoke to about. Then we'll see -- [overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Time is limited. Do you think it's -- [overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, well, I would like -- well, you know, I met with my colleague. I'm trying to -- not to lead the witness in any way and that is why I'm being so broad, but I will try to be more direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: It's your judgement call, but you'll note the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, did you meet with the Prosecution before you testified in The Hague? Simply, whether you met with the Prosecution before your testimony in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes. I met representatives of the OTP. They have an office in Belgrade, and I gave a statement to them. I spoke to them for two days, and that's when I gave a statement. And about your earlier question, I worked with the Mrksic Defence extensively. I was willing to testify in favour of any of the accused or testify for the OTP. I don't mind whose witness I am, because what I care about is that the truth is spoken here. I have been willing to testify. It was that way before and it's the same way now. That's why I'm here. I did work with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, it is established on the record that you testified on two occasions in Belgrade. You recall that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes. I testified before the special tribunal in Belgrade, where proceedings are underway against persons accused of committing murders at Ovcara, 16 of them. I testified two times before the Trial Chamber. There I provided answers to some 15 lawyers there and even the accused had the right to put questions to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, sir, my next question is quite simple. While you met with all of the persons you just spoke about, the Prosecution, the Mrksic Defence, or proceedings in Belgrade, did anyone at any time ask you questions about the contents of the conversation between Mrksic and Sljivancanin on the 20 November 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Nobody has ever asked me anything about the conversation between Commander Mrksic and Major Sljivancanin on the 20th of November at 8.00 p.m. at the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let us move to 20 November 1991. Can you describe briefly what were the activities that Operational Group South was involved on that day, very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: 20th of November, 1991, was day two after the fiercest fighting had ceased in the town of Vukovar. We were facing a great number of tasks and commitments at this time. The situation that some of the people faced during the actual combat was actually easier than the one they now found themselves facing when peace was back in town. All of a sudden we were swamped by a huge number of civilians who had just left their shelters and were now seeking our assistance. They wanted to go back to Croatia, Serbia, or Bosnia and Herzegovina. There were a number of tasks that had to do with the evacuation of the wounded. There were tasks that had to do with the future activities of our unit. It was a very dynamic situation. The reason the 20th of November really sticks in my mind is the evacuation of the hospital that took place as well as the government meeting that occurred in Vukovar at the time. I do remember a number of other details and any account that I may provide depends on how much time we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, let me take you immediately to the evening of 20 November 1991. I'd like to know if you were at the OG South command that night?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What time did you arrive at the command and what did you do then?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: I arrived at about 1600 hours. I had visited Ovcara previously before I met General -- or rather, Commander Mrksic. When I met Commander Mrksic, I briefed him in the shortest possible terms on what I had been doing that day and where I'd been to. I told him that I'd been to the barracks, the government meeting, that I'd been to Ovcara to try and take in the situation. I had briefed him on it in the shortest possible terms, and then I stayed at the command post throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, was there a daily briefing that day; and if so, at what time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Indeed, there was a daily briefing on that day, as there had been one on previous days. Normally it would start at 1800 hours, and this day was no different.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And who chaired the daily briefing and who was present, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes. Commander Mrksic chaired these briefings. Also in attendance were most of the other commanders and his assistants. Some were away because they had to deal with the evacuation of civilians, or rather, trying to get the civilian convoy on buses out of the town and towards destinations somewhere along the border or elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, do you recall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Bourgon, my colleague Judge Guney would like to ask a question. Judge Guney.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Panic, what was your personal interest at the time and what was your capacity and how can you remember all the details of the conversation that occurred between Mr. Mrksic and Mr. Sljivancanin? What's your interest in remembering all this? Could you tell us what your personal interest in remembering all this can be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time I was Chief of Staff of the Guards Brigade and also OG South in that particular area. I was Commander Mrksic's deputy. I'd stand-in for him when he was away. I was there for all the important tasks and for all the important briefings. I always directly witnessed whatever was going on. The only interest I have is the fact that I was, myself, carrying out a task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General Panic, quickly, do you recall what was discussed at the daily briefing that day?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Indeed I do. I've also been looking at documents in preparation for this testimony. Several key tasks were discussed on that day. It was about the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry to interrupt. I'm not quite sure what the relevance of the content of the daily briefing was. What we're concerned about in this hearing is the content of the conversation between Mr. Mrksic, Mr. Sljivancanin, and in the presence of Mr. Panic. I don't see in the scope of the context of this hearing what relevance there is to the content of the daily briefing, which has been fully litigated in the Tribunals below.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I suppose you are getting there, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I thank my colleague for that. I hope he will remember the same when he does his cross-examination, but I can move immediately after the briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What time does Mr. Sljivancanin arrive at the OG South that night, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin arrived at about 2000 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Who was present at the command when he arrived?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: I was there, Lieutenant-Colonel Trifunovic was there, and two signals officers were there too. I'm certain about these persons, but there may have been other people there too, some people processing documents, perhaps one of the operatives. And then occasionally other people would drop in, warrant officers who would bring mail or take mail away for delivery.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, sir, describe what happened exactly to the best of your recollection when Major Sljivancanin arrived at the OG South command.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: What I remember is I was seated at my table at the time, and Mr. Mrksic was there. He made a habit of pacing up and down the room when he wasn't doing anything in particular. It was in the operations room and he would walk from wall to wall, see what the signals men were doing. Sljivancanin is a tall man and stalwart, too, so he stood across the way from the commander somewhere near the door. He then spoke to him, "Colonel, sir, I'm just back from the hospital. I have completed my mission. Please, sir, can you tell me what exactly happened. I only know that a decision was taken in relation to the paramilitaries who were at the hospital. Why were they taken to Mitrovica but to Ovcara instead?" Mrksic gave no more than a brief reply. He said, "This was the government's call. There was a government meeting today and they took that decision. Make sure you remember your tasks in relation to tomorrow, and we can go back to discussing this later on."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note that there's a problem with the translation in terms of what was said by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, I will just read you one sentence that was on the transcript here, and you can tell me -- you can correct me if this is what you said. It says -- the question was what Sljivancanin said and then you said, "Colonel, sir, I'm just back from the hospital. I have completed my mission. Please, sir, can you tell me what exactly happened." And then that sentence here is the one I'm trying to get at. "I only know that a decision was taken in relation to the paramilitaries who were at the hospital. Why were they taken to Mitrovica but to Ovcara instead?" Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: No, no. I'll repeat. The moment Mr. Sljivancanin briefed General Mrksic to tell him that he was now back from the hospital, having completed his mission there, without even pausing he asked him the following question, "What happened, why was the decision changed so the members of the paramilitary units at the hospital who were hiding there did not go to Mitrovica, but went to Ovcara instead?" Mrksic then said, "This is a government decision. There was a government meeting today and they took this decision. We'll talk about that later."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, what else was discussed in that conversation to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Mrksic told him, "Listen, Sljivo," because that's what he used to call him, "the 80th Brigade would be taking charge of the zone of responsibility around these parts. The Guards Brigade would be on its way back to the Belgrade garrison. Tomorrow morning there is a large group of both domestic and foreign journalists arriving, about 120 journalists. Give Panic a hand just to make sure things go smoothly. I will not be around because I will be on my way to Belgrade to see federal secretary." And if I may just make a remark here, he even said, "Please don't push it in terms of how much you show your face before the journalists."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, where exactly were Mrksic and Sljivancanin in the room compared to where you were at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: It was all happening right next to me near the door to the room in which the command was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, were you a party to that conversation?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: No, I did not contribute myself. I was busy doing something and I just happened to be there and listened to that conversation. I was interested in hearing what they were talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, did you hear that conversation?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And on what basis can you say that you heard that conversation?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Well, because I was nearby. They were talking loud. Anyone who knows Mrksic knows that he talks loud and Sljivancanin talks even louder.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, during that conversation, was the situation of prisoners of war held at Ovcara discussed in any way?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: No, there was no discussion of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, it's been a long time. How can you be so sure?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: I'm sure. I just am. Had I not been sure about it, I would not have gotten in touch with Mr. Lukic to begin with and I certainly would not be sitting here today. I'm sure. Maybe I'm unable to remember every single word of that exchange after all this time. I'm sure that I don't. But I'm certain about one thing: What was not said. And that is what moved me to take steps. I'm obeying my conscience in coming up just to say this: It is simply not true that Mrksic told Sljivancanin at any point in time that he had withdrawn or indeed issued approval for the security detail to be withdrawn from Ovcara. I could keep telling you the same thing any time of day or night and no matter who asks. Perhaps I'm unable to remember every single word or detail. I'll grant you that. I may have heard these things. I may not remember all of them right now, but this is not the sort of thing that would slip your mind --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Why not --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: -- this is something that is essential and directly affects the security of the people who were at Ovcara. After I came back from Ovcara, I briefed Mrksic on what the situation was like there. I said, "Step-up the security." I said, "Dispatch more people there to give Vojnovic a hand, in a technical sense, if necessary," although he had sufficient men who were there already and soldiers. Mrksic agreed and as far as I remember he dispatched a contingent there. I think I testified about this the last time around. Captain Bozic was also at Ovcara and someone else from the security body. Following my briefing to Mrksic. That is why I'm saying what I'm saying. At no point did he tell Sljivancanin anything like that. If he had told Sljivancanin, he certainly would have told me in my capacity as Chief of Staff. I was after all his deputy and I was there with him throughout. That is the gist of it. I do apologise if perhaps I've -- if I spoke a little louder and strictly necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, I would like to ask a question of clarification, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: By all means, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: A moment ago Mr. Panic said, and I'm quoting from the transcript "I was busy doing something," he was busy during the meeting between Mr. Mrksic and Mr. Sljivancanin. And my question to the witness is whether you can remember any details of this conversation between Mrksic and Sljivancanin, apart from the fact that Mrksic did not inform Sljivancanin about the withdrawal, or is this the only item that remained in your mind? Because to clarify, in your testimony during trial and in your previous statements, you did not testify in an affirmative manner on anything that was said or not said during the conversation between Sljivancanin and Mrksic. So please tell us how you can suddenly remember so clearly that the withdrawal of JNA protection was not mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was sitting there busy doing something. Sljivancanin was to my right. I stopped working for a moment. The two of them met in the room, standing across the way from each other, and I was listening to their conversation. I do allow for the possibility that I don't remember every single detail of that conversation. I do know, however, what the general drift was. When Sljivancanin came he said, "I'm back from the hospital. I've completed my mission." And went on to ask Mrksic how the change had come about in terms of the paramilitaries who were at the hospital and selected there being sent to Sremska Mitrovica, but that was changed and they were now to be sent to Ovcara. Why was that changed? Mrksic said, "The government met today. It was a decision that they took. This is something we'll be discussing in due course." Why do I remember this? Simply because the following day Sljivancanin was with me and we were supposed to carry out a specific task, a regular task, to do with the transport of civilians and a number of other routine steps. There was still sporadic fighting in some places. I also know for a fact that Mrksic gave him a number of specific tasks. Now, this is very important. He had to know this. The zone of responsibility was passing into the hands of the 80th Brigade and the Guards Brigade will be on its way back. This is essential. It's not something one would be likely to forget. It's always there in one's mind. They would be on their way back to the Belgrade garrison, and he would be assisting me the next day when this large group of journalists would be arriving, for those people to be welcomed and for the whole thing to be organised in addition to all our routine tasks, as I said. Had Mrksic told Sljivancanin something like this: I issued approval or even ordered for the security detail from Ovcara to be withdrawn, I would have been the first to react in my capacity as an officer, Chief of Staff, his own deputy, and first and foremost as a human being. I would have said something along these lines: Commander, it wasn't like that, not until a minute ago. What has come up? And I'm certain that Mr. Sljivancanin, as chief of security, would have done the very same thing. I know because I was at Ovcara myself. I briefed that commander; and no more than an hour before, he had agreed. This kind of conversation would have stuck with me for the rest of my life, just as I clearly remember that no such thing was ever uttered. As I said, had something like this been uttered, I would have been the first to react.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Judge Vaz has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Panic, you told us earlier that you arrived at the command post at 4.00 p.m. on November 20th and that you stayed until the end. Could you tell us exactly what means "till the end." What time was it when you left the command post, if you left it? Where was Sljivancanin at that time when you left? And the future missions were also mentioned and you just talked about it. Could you tell us exactly in the framework of this conversation between Mrksic and Sljivancanin regarding these future missions, what exactly was Mrksic's answer when Sljivancanin asked him what he was supposed to do the next days. I'm sorry, I'm a bit hoarse at the moment, but I hope that you understood my question, otherwise I can repeat, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Vaz. Mr. Panic, the question was clear to you, right? Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question is clear. Just in order to make sure we understand this, the mainstay of the activity at the command post would take place in this room that we called the operations room. There would be a number of officers who were there throughout. I was there, the commander was there whenever we were not touring the units. I arrived at 1600 hours that evening, having completed all my daily tasks. I briefed the commander and sat down at my own desk. I was there throughout, in that room at the command post. Right across from there there was a recreation room that we had there, and that was where I would spend my nights before we were off to new missions. But I do understand what you are after. At no point in time did I actually physically leave during their conversation, simply because the conversation was brief. As for the specific tasks that Mrksic handed out to Sljivancanin, I'll repeat, one was that the 80th Brigade would be taking charge of the zone of responsibility. He was telling him this because Sljivancanin had not attended the daily briefing when this was discussed and when the commander of the 80th Brigade assumed responsibility. It was very important for Sljivancanin, as chief of security, to be aware of this, that he would have other commitments soon probably now that this new brigade was taking over. Secondly, the Guards Brigade would be on its way back to the Belgrade garrison which was essential for him as security chief, because that would enable him to plan his own security tasks and assignments in this complex situation where we suddenly faced 12.000 civilians coming to us, begging us to help them out, to give them something to eat and to take them as far as the border or wherever they wanted to go. Another task was in relation to the next day. As I said, Sljivancanin was very much in the public eye, in the media. Nevertheless, he was the security chief and he had to vouch for the safety of a large group of domestic and foreign journalists in a situation that was as riotous as this one was. They would be there the following morning and Sljivancanin was told to give me a hand with this task, just to make sure that everything went smoothly. These journalists eventually arrived, a press conference was organised and held, and perhaps that is also something that we can bring up if necessary. That's in the briefest of terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Panic. You told us that this conversation on the question that we're interested in today was very short, but could you give us some information as to the length of this conversation. Was it possible to revisit the issue? You said that you stayed there all the time and -- or most of the time, but could you imagine that at one point in time maybe Mr. Mrksic could have told Sljivancanin what we are interested about today, i.e., what -- about the security detail that was supposed to be withdrawn. Do you think that at one point in time this could have been mentioned between the two without you overhearing it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll say this again. I was right there, in close physical proximity, and the conversation was short. Maybe over a minute, but it certainly wasn't longer than five- to ten-minutes, their encounter. It would not have been feasible for Mrksic to tell him that without me hearing it. For the most part, I heard everything they said. Granted, I may not be able to remember every single word and it has been a long time. Nevertheless, what I'm telling you is: I heard everything there and then. And I assert, had he ever said anything about the security detail being withdrawn and had I heard that, I would have been the first to react. This would have constituted an important reversal in this whole situation as well as a violation of something that the two of us had agreed on shortly before when I had briefed him on the situation at Ovcara. It was clear that this would have constituted a threat to the safety of the people at Ovcara, and I wouldn't have glossed over it, no way. I don't think this possibly could have happened. He couldn't possibly have told Sljivancanin because we were all there at all times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, sorry, just a short follow-up question to the question asked by my distinguished colleague, Judge Vaz. Do you remember, Mr. Panic, or don't you, when Mr. Sljivancanin asked Mr. Mrksic about these future missions, is this among the things that remained in your memory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sljivancanin was not seeking missions. He listened to the tasks that Mrksic was giving to him. So I repeat, Mr. Sljivancanin arrived, reported about what he had done and where he had been, and Mrksic gives him tasks after that. If necessary, I can repeat all the details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Do help us, Mr. Bourgon, didn't Mr. Sljivancanin testify that he asked Mrksic about his future missions? And I'm trying simply to identify whether the witness remembers that scrap of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I think Mr. Lukic has also that recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, of course it's on the record of what Mr. Sljivancanin said during his testimony. What you have today is what Mr. Panic remembers. If there are differences, there are differences, and the Appeals Chamber will have to draw the consequences of any differences. But it's been 19 years, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: No, no, I understand that. Would you like to add to your answer to me, Mr. Panic? Because if there is -- if there is this item of the conversation that you do not remember, it could conceivably be true that there are other fragments that you do not remember or have not heard. I would be grateful for any help on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I guess this will be covered in detail in cross-examination, what the witness remembers from the conversation he mentioned in detail to the Appeals Chamber. I think he will stick to his story, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not sure it's for Mr. Bourgon to comment upon what the witness will say. Your Honours asked a question and I think the Court's entitled -- and I would very much like to hear the answer to the questions that Your Honours posed, even if my learned friend does not wish to hear the answers that Your Honours have -- the question -- the answer to the question, so perhaps we could hear from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I believe, Mr. President, it is indeed very important. I can either ask the question or you can ask, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General Panic, Mr. Sljivancanin said in his testimony that he inquired about what his next duties would be. Is that how it took place?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: That's possible. It's possible that that's what happened. It's possible. I accept that it's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: But you do not have a recollection of that or do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember -- I remember tasks. At that moment, whether Sljivancanin had asked something, that's a detail that -- well, it's possible that he asked him something that I missed. It's possible after all these years that I'm missing something, but I did hear the gist of the conversation -- or rather, I remember the gist of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I just have two more questions, Mr. President. I know I'm out of time, but I have two more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, who was -- after that conversation, who was the first to leave the room?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: After that conversation, the first to leave the room was Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And where did he go, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Well, he went to that place, Negoslavci, he had his command -- or rather, security organs in house number 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, after that conversation that you just described, were there any more exchange of words between Mrksic and Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Well, I noted what it was that remained carved in my memory and that I certainly could not forget. It's possible that they exchanged another word or two. It's possible. But I doubt that I missed it. It was a brief conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But after that conversation, did they speak again? That's my simple question. Did they speak again after?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. Mr. Sljivancanin left the room. Mr. Mrksic was still with me there, and after a while Mr. Mrksic left too. I think that he went to visit our wounded at the hospital in Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And my last question: That press conference that you mentioned, did that press conference take place the next day?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That conference was held at the barracks in Vukovar. At that conference, as I've already mentioned, there were 120 journalists from home and abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, can you just turn to your tab 7 in your binder. There's a picture there. I'd like you to describe that picture for us. Do you recognise this picture?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I recognise this picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: This is a room, or rather, a classroom, the biggest room in the barracks where we received the journalists and where the press conference was held on the 21st of November in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Is Mr. Sljivancanin present on this picture?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Sljivancanin is present. He's right in front of the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Who was the centre of attention during that press conference?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: At the press conference, regardless of the fact that it was chaired by our organ for morale and political work, the journalists expressed the greatest interest in Mr. Sljivancanin, and he was the media personality on that day as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And are you present in that picture, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am. I am in that picture. I'm in the second row and I'm standing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This concludes your examination. I am told by the technical department that changing the tapes requires 20 rather than 15 minutes. So we will meet here at quarter to 11.00 sharp. The court will now rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please be seated. Okay. We will now have cross-examination of Mr. Panic by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: And you have one hour and 15 minutes, and do start.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Good morning, General. My name's Paul Rogers. I'm appearing on behalf of the Prosecution and I will be conducting the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: General, you told us in evidence that you became aware of the appeals judgement and as a result of that you contacted Mr. Lukic the same day or the next morning; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: The next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Having had, I think, a sleepless night, the way you've described it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: And when you were able to speak with Mr. Lukic, he suggested that it would be helpful for him to know a number of facts; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: In particular, you told us that in that first conversation what he wanted to know was whether you were present; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Who else was there; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: And what you spoke about; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: And in particular, what was said between Mr. Sljivancanin and Mr. Mrksic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: I asked Mr. Lukic to confirm to me whether what I had seen was correct, what I learned from that judgement, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: My question was: Mr. Lukic wanted to know from you what you could say about the conversation between Mr. Mrksic and Mr. Sljivancanin; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic said to me or explained to me that that was correct, that that is what the verdict was passed for. And then there was my reaction, namely, that I was there and that I cannot accept that that was correct. He told me to wait for his return.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: General, it was a very simple question. I'll put it to you one more time. When you spoke with Mr. Lukic, he particularly wanted to know what you could say about the conversation between Mr. Sljivancanin and Mr. Mrksic; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Well, he was interested in -- well, he wanted me to think about what it was that I remembered in relation to that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And you already said that in your evidence at 092949. I just wanted to make it clear that we were in agreement, that he did want you to recollect your conversation. He told you, I understand it, that you should keep it to yourself; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: When you first met with Mr. Lukic and before you made your statement, when you went through your account did Mr. Lukic make any notes of what you said that you recall?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Well, he didn't take any notes then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Okay. So you met again some months later or around the 8th of October, 2009, to provide your actual statement; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: We met once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes. And you said you were provided -- forgive me.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We met once again a few months later, and then our third encounter was when I signed the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: And you told us that you were provided with some guide-lines for making your statement; that's right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, just some guide-lines so that I do not speak at too great a length.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: And you told us that they were provided to you in a form of sort of bullet points. Was this written down?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: He said that to me. It was oral, rather, and I just jotted down a few things for myself, this, that, and the other thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Thank you. And you told us what he asked for. Now, my note of your evidence this morning was this, he asked you: "What I was, where I was, and to write down what I had heard in the contents, that is, the contents of the conversation." That's what he asked you to do, those were your instructions, is that right, to write down the content of the conversation in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was it. Then, also why I did not speak about that earlier and why I decided to testify or why I accepted to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: So you agree that one of the primary purposes of your statement was to put your fullest recollection of the events outlined in that conversation down on paper; you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the briefest possible terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes. Brief, you say, but nevertheless you needed to deal with the totality of the conversation that had happened between Mr. Mrksic and Mr. Sljivancanin; you agree with that? That was the purpose of the statement, after all.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: My understanding was that the purpose of the statement was, in addition to stating my own particulars and the fact that I already testified, that I was supposed to say what the basic things were that had been said by Mrksic and Sljivancanin when they met and that I was prepared to testify in order to be able to clarify during the testimony. So here I am and please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: So the purpose was to try to recall as much as you possibly could about that conversation and put it down in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. That's not it. Had he said that to me, that statement would have been very detailed and it would have been over 20 pages long. It was supposed to be short. The statement was supposed to be short containing only the basic questions that I could testify about. When you look at it, it was written up on two pages, handwritten.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: And the totality of what you recorded in your original statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Bourgon is on his feet. I wonder if he's got an objection or --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd just like to -- because we're going for more than one hour here, and if my colleague is going to suggest something to the witness, that's one thing. But he should not say something that the witness said that the witness did not say. In this case, he said - not as a suggestion - but he said that it was for you to remember -- he said -- I'm looking for the words here, the exact words. "So the purpose was to try to recall as much as you possibly could about the conversation." Now, that's not what the witness had said earlier. So I just want my colleague to stick to the answers or to make it as a suggestion. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Bourgon. It is a suggestion when you read it. It's a proper cross-examination question to put a suggestion as to what the purpose was and my learned friend perfectly well knows that it is a proper question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, you've told us that the purpose was to provide a more broad outline, I think, and the outline you provided was this - and I'm going to read to you -- that's Exhibit RD6, it's a Defence document. There's no need for you to turn to it because I'm just going to read it to you. It's the seventh paragraph on the page. You said this - and if anyone wants to correct me, they can: "During this conversation Mrksic informed Sljivancanin that the Guards Brigade would be going back to brigade and that the 80th Motorised Brigade would assume responsibility in the area. Mrksic also told Sljivancanin that he should assist me the next day by handling the large number media who were expected in Vukovar, which was an important task for all members of the command. At no time during this conversation did Mrksic inform Sljivancanin that members of the military police of the 80th Motorised Brigade had been ordered to withdraw from that location, i.e., Ovcara." That's the totality of what you recorded about the conversation on the 8th of October. Today, you have provided for the first time much more detail about those events; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: And you've told us a number of things relating to what Mr. Sljivancanin appeared to have said. For example, that he'd just come back from the hospital, having completed his mission; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: That's not anywhere recorded in your written statement, is it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: It was not recorded in my written statement because I have the possibility of stating that here, live.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: There's no reference in your written statement to the -- anything to do with the hand-over of the prisoners, even to the government session. There's no reference in there at all to the government session and any orders that the government session may have given?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: No, there is no reference to that in the statement. I testified about that here today. I testified about that session, about the decisions, at the previous testimony here, when I appeared here to testify earlier on, in 1996 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: My understanding of your evidence is that the first time that you were asked to recall anything about this conversation or to provide any details about this conversation was when you first met with Mr. Lukic for the purpose of this appeals process, for the -- is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: The first time I met with Mr. Lukic, I discussed that a bit more. And I told him about certain details from that meeting between Mrksic and Sljivancanin. And he said to me, "Let that be and in time we will see whether we're going to do anything with that, anything further." It was my understanding that he was supposed to carry out some investigations or some kind of procedure -- well, not investigation, but to gather more information. I mean, I'm not the only one who was there during those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: When you spoke with the Office of the Prosecutor and provided your statement on the -- or about the 1st of September, 2005, you were asked about the evening briefing and you were asked about whether the hospital evacuation was discussed. And you said: "I do not recall whether Major Sljivancanin spoke about the evacuation of the hospital at the briefing, but I assume he did inform Mrksic." And that's in your OTP statement, which is RP16 at page 24, paragraph 88. Do you recall telling the OTP that in your statement, that you assumed he did inform Mrksic? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: I worked with the OTP for two days.
