I made a statement and it is noted in that statement that I do not recall that he spoke -- I mean, the reference is to the evening briefing at 1800 hours. As I prepared later for that testimony in 2006 and for this testimony as well, as I was leafing through the war diary and other documents, and as I was trying to refresh my memory, of course things had been different. Sljivancanin was not -- well, I mean, that's why I said that I did not remember that he had said anything. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: No, but you see, General, you said that I assume he did inform Mrksic about the hospital evacuation. But the fact is that you knew that not only did you assume it, you knew he had done that because you were present, you say, at the meeting subsequently where that very topic was discussed, i.e., the subject of this hearing. So why did you say "I assume he informed Mrksic," when in fact you knew, according to your evidence, that he had informed Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, when he arrived and when they met he said, "I have accomplished my task at the hospital." That's what is true, but it's not in the statement for the following reason: I gave that statement unprepared at the time. I made the statement when I personally had some major psychological and physical trouble of my own. And I went to see the Prosecution and talk to them when my wife was dying of cancer. Unfortunately she died immediately after that. The situation was such that at that point in time I could have missed some facts because I was troubled by problems of my own at the time. It is possible that that was an omission on my part. I accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: General, you were cross-examined during the course of your testimony in the trial, and you were asked about whether you remembered making your OTP statement. And at transcript 14485 to 90 you said that you made changes to virtually every page of the OTP statement because "there were both mistakes in terms of content, style, language, typographical errors, and so on." That's 14485, lines 25 to 3 -- 485 or 6, 25 to 3. This was something that should have been corrected, according to you, in relation to its content, shouldn't it because it's wrong? You didn't assume, you knew, and you had ample opportunity to change it but you didn't.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: For two days I was giving my statement and it was shown to me. I corrected some things I thought had to be corrected. I'm telling you what the situation was like. It is possible that I omitted some things, that I didn't correct everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: General, your recollection of events would appear to be improving over time rather than getting worse, wouldn't it? After 19 years, it seems to be much better than it was when you were giving your OTP statement. You're filling in more details today even than you had done previously, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Well, I apologise for saying this, but this is a bit sarcastic. It is possible that with time and with age memory gets worse, deteriorates. But it's a fact that after testifying in 2006 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction:

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That for my testimony in 2006 and for this testimony, I devoted some time to preparation and I thought about some particular matters. Here this is about the fate of people. That is something for which a sufficient amount of facts and evidence is necessary, and I prepared for that. I leafed through some documents, the war diary. I refreshed my memory. But I agree with you that as time passes we don't get any younger.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: You were also given an opportunity during the course of your evidence in chief at the trial to expand upon the conversation between Mr. Mrksic and Mr. Sljivancanin. If I refer you to your evidence on the 9th of November, 2006, at trial transcript 14330, lines 1 to 7, you said this when you were being asked about Sljivancanin: "Of course Sljivancanin was given time to say something at all meetings." The context is that you were talking about the briefing. "Of course, Sljivancanin was given time to say something at all meetings, to say things, to ask things. I don't remember that he was present," that is, at the briefing, "because I certainly would have remembered what it was that he would have said about what he did at the hospital. As far as I can remember, he came somewhat later to the command post. It was dark. In all fairness, at 1800 hours, it's dark, too." I think he came, "around 2000 hours, and I know that he talked to the commander." And there you stopped and nothing more was said about that conversation. You had an opportunity then, didn't you, to explain what you're explaining now?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I would have been glad if someone had asked me then. Maybe there would be no need for us to sit here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Forgive me, my understanding of your evidence is that the first time that anybody had raised this question of that conversation with you was when these matters came to be dealt with on appeal; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Judge Pocar has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Rogers, you gave an answer given by the witness at the hearing in 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Which was exactly the question that was put to the witness on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can find that. The question was: "Do you remember specifically whether Sljivancanin attended that meeting," that is, the briefing, "whether he said something, whether he reported, do you have any memory of that and did you see him that evening at all?" And then came the answer: "Of course Sljivancanin was given time to say something at meetings ..." et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Panic, my question was: My understanding of your evidence is that you told us the first time that you were given an opportunity to speak about these events, the first time it became necessary to speak about these events or tell anyone about it, was at the appeals stage; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. But allow me to explain why. Giving evidence here and before the special tribunal and making a series of statements, nobody ever asked me about the content of the conversation between Mrksic and Sljivancanin -- or, in other words, at the -- that Mrksic withdrew the security detail from Ovcara and that he gave that information to Sljivancanin was never asked or stated before. That's why I'm saying --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Okay. I think the witness was asked to repeat the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So as nobody ever asked me, as I said, on how many occasions giving evidence or making statements, I never spoke about that until the moment when I saw something impossible: My commander making the decision to withdraw the security detail, informs me about that decision, and I react [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: I understand. And I'm curious, did you ever mention the conversation of the meeting to Mr. Lukic or to the team defending Mr. Sljivancanin during the course of the trial?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Well, no. I repeat, that conversation was the consequence of this verdict -- or rather, I came forward because Mr. Sljivancanin was sentenced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It's an important correction on the transcript. At page 51, lines 6 and 7, it says here on the transcript: "Informs me about that decision and I react." And what the witness really said is "did not inform me about that decision." So I think we need to correct that before we move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: My question, Mr. Panic, is this, and I wonder whether you can help - maybe you can't - but the Prosecution was provided with a proofing note of what evidence you could give prior to your testimony at the trial. That's at RP17. And in that proofing note on the second page, the penultimate paragraph, says this: "The witness was present at the regular reporting at Colonel Mrksic's on 20 November 1991 at 1800 hours. Sljivancanin was not present at the meeting, but later, after the meeting, he was present when Sljivancanin and Mrksic were having the conversation." It would seem, Mr. Panic, that you had previously mentioned the content of the conversation or the fact at least of the conversation between Mr. Sljivancanin and Mrksic at an earlier stage and that this very question as to what was in that statement -- as to what you could say was dealt with. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: There's a note that was provided as to your potential evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Do you want to -- when you complete the point that you're continuing, Judge Guney will have a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So I will just let you finish this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, I just want to explain it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, so you understand, there is a note provided as to what you may have testified about at trial, was given to the lawyers in advance of your testimony at trial. In that note, there is a reference to what you could say about a meeting at which Sljivancanin and Mrksic were present, "having the conversation" is what it says, all right? So you understand. So my point is for you to comment upon: This would seem to suggest that you had in fact discussed the content of that conversation before your testimony and it wasn't the first time you dealt with it. A matter for you to comment.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes. Before putting down my statement on paper, I did speak to Mr. Lukic about the content of the conversation between Mr. Mrksic and Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think it's a question for comment at the end of the day. I've given the witness an opportunity to comment upon it. It may be he can't make a remark about what other people might have written, but it's there. He's had an opportunity. That's the only reason for putting it to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: We interrupt you, Mr. Rogers. Now Judge Guney then Judge Pocar -- yes, before the question of Judge Guney or --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Or if you want to --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, it is directly related to the last question that was asked by my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Then by all means do it now and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I apologise to Judge Guney. It's just that my colleague, when he read from the proofing note, he mentioned -- and I will quote the exact line. I just have to stop the transcript here. And he said that "you were given an opportunity." I quote from page 52 at line 22 where it says: "What you may have testified about at trial was given to the lawyers in advance of your testimony at trial." Then it says: "In that note there is a reference to what you could say about a meeting ..." and this is not what is in the proofing note. What the proofing note says - and Your Honours have this in the tab before you - it simply says that after the meeting he was present when Sljivancanin and Mrksic were having the conversation. So we should not try to lead the witness into answering a question on something that was not in the proofing note. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Do you want quickly to respond to that before --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The implication --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: -- we move to Judge Guney?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: The implication of the proofing note is that -- and this is why it may be more a matter for comment than for the witness, but the implication in the proofing note is that the witness was in a position to explain the content of that conversation because it's referred to within the proofing note. So that was the point. And as I say, it may be more a matter for comment, but I felt it was fair to the witness to give him an opportunity himself to comment upon that but there it is. I think we can leave it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Judge Guney, I appreciate your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: We're not having any French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I repeat my question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Do we have interpretation now, or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: We have it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So do kindly repeat the question, Judge Guney, just to play it safe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why did Mrksic not mention the order to withdraw the troops during this conversation with Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's the crucial matter. At my previous testimony, and now too, I can say that I know Mrksic very well. He's a good commander. And if he made that decision, to withdraw the security detail from Ovcara, he should have informed me, being his Chief of Staff and being involved in the carrying out of his orders. He should have informed the other members of the command if he made that decision. Mrksic simply didn't inform anybody about it. Whether he made that decision or not, I don't know, but I repeat, that's a decision that only the commander can make. It's the commander's authority to withdraw an order that he gave before. I never heard of such a decision. I didn't hear him saying that to Sljivancanin, and that's why I'm here in front of you to speak about that fact in the presence of God.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, let me follow this up. We do know -- you do know that the security detail was withdrawn, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I learned that rather late, that the security detail had been withdrawn or that they were under some pressure or that they -- that they had gone due to the action of some strange forces. But I only heard about that after returning to Belgrade, which is what I said before this Tribunal. I didn't hear and couldn't believe that Mrksic on that evening issued that order to anyone. He didn't order it to me or in my presence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. The military -- the security detail was, of course, withdrawn, and we are talking of movement of military forces. You were the Chief of Staff of General Mrksic -- of Colonel Mrksic at that time, and you have no theory to offer? It was not an act of God the troops were withdrawn. How do you explain that withdrawal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, when I testified here in 2006 I remember well that I said, "Whoever answers the question who ordered the withdrawal of the security detail or who withdrew them on his own initiative and jeopardised the security of those people at Ovcara, that is the crux of the matter when it comes to the fate of the people at Ovcara." I repeat, I did not know about such a decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, you said that you gave additional details today relating to the content of that conversation, but you accept that your recollection may not be complete to all of the details of the conversation between Mrksic and Sljivancanin; you agree?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: I accept that I may have omitted something and that the passage of time has left some traces.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: See, when Mr. Sljivancanin testified about this meeting, one of the things that he mentioned was that the commander had told him that the government had taken charge of a group of suspects from the hospital that had been taken to the barracks in order for them to be later exchanged for captured Serbs. That's in the transcript 13655 to 6. You haven't made any mention in your evidence today relating to the reference to suspects from the hospital being taken to the barracks for exchange. Can you comment on that, please. Was it said?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes. I mentioned that in my testimony. You may have omitted it. Mr. Sljivancanin, when he met with Mrksic, said, "I'm coming from the hospital. I accomplished my mission. Commander, what happened that brought about the change of the decision? The members of the paramilitary units," and I mentioned to them -- referred to them as prisoners, when their unit surrendered at Mitnica, the people who surrendered knew that they hadn't committed any crimes and they were also at Ovcara. It was the night from between the 18th and the 19th. They spent the night there, and the security detail was the same, the same units of the 80th Brigade. On the following day they were taken to Sremska Mitrovica by buses. The other part of that unit, knowing that they were guilty of crimes, escaped in the direction of the hospital. They found refuge at the hospital. They lay in hospital beds. Some of them put plaster-casts on their arms, legs, or heads, and they were waiting to be evacuated as wounded soldiers under the auspices of the Red Cross and the international observers. And these people I call members of paramilitary units --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: General, that wasn't what I asked you. What I asked you was relating to what Mr. Sljivancanin testified about, that Mrksic had told him that the government had taken charge of a group of suspects from the hospital brought to the barracks in order to be later exchanged for captured Serbs. And you haven't made any mention at all in your testimony so far relating to that, asking you why. Was it said or wasn't it said?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: It was said. Let me continue. Sljivancanin asks Mrksic, "What happened that you changed your decision about these people not going to Mitrovica, but to Ovcara instead?" And Mrksic said, "Today there was a government session and this was a government decision, and we'll see about this later." This is what I stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what you stated, but what Mr. Sljivancanin suggested is that they were to be later exchanged for captured Serbs. That was his evidence before the Chamber, and I'm asking you whether you heard that, that these prisoners were allegedly going to be exchanged for captured Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: With your leave, the first group I was speaking about went to Sremska Mitrovica and there was an all-for-all exchange, and they are alive even today, thank God. The other group, in line with the same methodology should have been exchanged, but the government insisted that they would be tried. That was the only difference. And Mr. Sljivancanin maybe spoke about it at more length than I. The difference may be in the length of the answer, but not in the essence. In essence, we're saying the same. They were also supposed to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: But your evidence at trial, which was rejected by the Trial Chamber on this point, but your evidence at trial was that they were to be tried, not exchanged, to be tried. And here apparently Mrksic is telling Sljivancanin that they're to be exchanged, in complete contradiction to what you understood the position to be. What do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Well, I can speak about that if the Trial Chamber has enough time. I can speak about this extensively because I was present at the government session. The -- on the 20th of November, there was a government session, I was present, and I heard their conclusion. I related them to Mrksic, Mrksic accepted --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: General, General, it's a very simple question and it relates directly to what was said in the meeting, and you are avoiding answering the question, I suggest to you. There's no reference made by you in your testimony to exchange for Serbs until recently, until I've just put it to you. Now, I'm suggesting that in your original account, in the account that you gave today, you haven't referred to any reference to exchange for captured Serbs. That's right? And that would be in contradiction to what you understood was to be happening to them, namely, that they were to be tried; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes. The decision was made at the government session that they would be tried, and I can go into the details regarding that government session and the conclusions made there. And Mrksic accepted their decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: That account that you gave, that there was to be trials, was rejected by the Trial Chamber as untrue, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: And you're repeating it again now, you still stand by that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Well, allow me to explain --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: No, you just have to say is --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: -- how this came about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: All you have to do is say whether you stand by your original trial testimony or not on this point, that they were to be tried.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: I stand by what I said, that this was a government decision which was also accepted by Mrksic that they would be tried, brought to justice. The prime minister on that day after the government session made a public statement on TV and said, "Today a government session was held, at which it was decided that these persons from the hospital should be tried. Whoever has blood on his hands will be convicted; who is innocent will be set free." And he stated that publicly on television. The then-prime minister of a country which was recognised at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Do you agree that --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Does Mr. Bourgon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Is there a problem, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, I'd just like to have a reference. My colleague said that the Trial Chamber had rejected, and he said exactly these words: "That account that you gave, that there was to be trials, was rejected by the Trial Chamber as untrue ..." I would just like to have a reference because that's not what I recall from the judgement, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Could we have the chapter and verse on that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Trial judgement, paragraph 307 said: "While the Chamber accepts that Panic arrived at Ovcara shortly after the arrival of the buses from the JNA barracks, it is unable to accept his explanation as to why he was at Ovcara. It is entirely lacking in credibility that he believed that trials of prisoners could be in progress at Ovcara. There was manifestly no time for this to be implemented, even had there been the necessary skilled investigators ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we're talking at that time as the reason why he went to Ovcara, not whether they were tried or not, that the intent was to try them or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, that was the -- that's the -- my learned friend can say as he wishes. That was my understanding of that passage. If it's wrong, it's wrong. But certainly his explanation as to why they were at Ovcara, that is, that they were to be tried -- that trials could even begin to be in progress, given against the background of the fact that the Chamber did not accept that there could be a functioning government at the time, would be -- would appear to be consistent, that this whole question of trials was simply not honest. But there we are. Perhaps again it's a matter for comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, you were telling us about the -- your account of what happened, and you told us that you were busy doing something. What was it that you were busy doing when Mr. Sljivancanin and Mr. Mrksic began to have their conversation?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: The daily briefing was through and the tasks had been handed out. The Chief of Staff and the staff - and this applies to all the armies throughout the world, it certainly applied to us - were elaborating on the commander's order and rephrasing it as an order for the units. They were making proposals to the commander for how the tasks -- on how the tasks would be carried out. Each of us were also working on our own personal preparation. Specifically, the tasks for that day were quite comprehensive --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: -- there were large numbers of civilians who needed to be taken care of --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: I understand --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: -- there was a different unit assuming responsibility. This had to be phrased in the form of an order. We had to prepare this unit for going back to the garrison, and I personally had to prepare for the press conference because my commander would not be there on the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: So the impression I'm getting is that this was a busy period of time in the operations room?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: There was a lot going on?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: And you told us that the conversation between Mr. Sljivancanin and Mr. Mrksic may have lasted certainly longer than a minute -- longer than a minute but not longer than five or ten minutes. So it could have been as long as five or ten minutes that these two individuals were conversing?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, I suggest to you that in the busy environment of the operations room, given the length of time that it appears these two were talking, there may well have been parts of the conversation that you simply missed, you didn't hear accurately or at all what was being said?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: At this point in time, I mean the briefing occurred at 1800 hours. The commanders and those who were involved in the briefing then left the room. Staying at the command post were me, the commander, Lieutenant-Colonel Trifunovic, and the signals men who were busy doing their own work. The tasks had already been handed out and were now under way. I wasn't the only person there performing all of these tasks. I divided out the tasks and I was working at this point in time on my own personal preparation in case the need arose for someone to consult me or submit anything to me for signature or, for example, if I was required to approve of a plan. I was sitting there at one point in time the door opens and Mrksic is pacing up and down. Do you want me to go into the physical detail of the situation? Between the window and the wall and they met, they came together, right next to my table and started talking. Sljivancanin is a man of monumental stature. I couldn't possibly have missed him, so I heard the conversation. I may have missed the occasional detail. Had I known what might later happen, I would have resorted to actually recording the conversation; but I didn't know at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Why would you have resorted to recording the conversation?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: So that today we would no longer be discussing whether I heard or indeed did not hear something. We would then have proof. I'll say this a thousand times over if that's what it takes: I cannot fathom that Mrksic produced an order like that, and I'll say this a million times. He never told that to anybody. He didn't tell me and he didn't tell Sljivancanin in my presence, and they were right next to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: You said that if you had heard such a thing, you would have been the first to react. Is that because you would have appreciated that the prisoners would have been in danger and you needed to act to protect them?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that question. As I said, I would have been the first to react. I would have sprung to my feet and ask him, "Commander, what's wrong with you? Why are you going back on your decision? Do you know that I was at Ovcara? Did I not brief you on that, on the situation there? Had we not agreed for security to be stepped-up? Had I not made my proposal to you that someone should be dispatched there to provide technical assistance" --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: General, General, I asked you: Would you have acted because you appreciated that the prisoners were in danger and you would have needed to act to protect them? As Chief of Staff, as an officer, you needed to act to protect them in the face of such an order, do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Well, absolutely. That's what I've been telling you all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: And that's why --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: The withdrawal of the security detail would have put the people in that prison in harm's way directly. There were criminals among those people there. And secondly, perhaps there were people around who might have wanted to take matters into their own hands and take revenge, retaliation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: If you failed to act, you yourself could have been at risk of punishment under the regulations under Articles 20 and 21 of your own military regulations; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. If there was something that I didn't do --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, which is why, General, you simply could never admit to hearing about the order for withdrawal during the course of that conversation. You could never come and give an account which involved that happening because it implicates you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes. From where you stand, that is correct; from where I stand -- had I been afraid for my own responsibility, I would never have gotten in touch with Mr. Lukic. Quite the contrary, I am doing my best for truth to emerge before this Trial Chamber. The best thing for us would be for Mr. Mrksic to say: I ordered this or I ordered something else, and I ordered this and that to such and such a person, so that the facts are established --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Or is it the case, General, that you want to come here today to try to set the record straight, as you call it, to ensure that there can be no implication on you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: No. During my testimony I said I was with those people, I was there. I was Chief of Staff. I know what went on. Please try to recognise the fact that Mrksic never ordered that to any of us. I failed to understand how he could possibly have ordered that to anyone at all, knowing Mrksic, knowing his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber, when it was considering your evidence in the quote below, rejected it on occasions when it appeared to them to be self-serving and in situations where you yourself were implicated in possible criminal behaviour, that's what they found. And they found in relation to one particular matter this at trial judgement paragraph 585, this is referring again to the government session planned to put war criminals on trial. And perhaps this is a better quote from the judgement than the one I referred Your Honours to earlier when I was making my submissions as to what was said. It said this: "In his evidence about the meeting," that's the SAO government meeting, "Lieutenant-Colonel Panic sought to say that from the debate at the meeting it appeared that the SAO government planned to put the war criminals on trial. While he indicated he believed this to be their intention when he conveyed Mile Mrksic's position, the Chamber is quite unable to accept the honesty of this aspect of his evidence. It was obviously self-serving, and also an attempt to put the JNA and Mile Mrksic in a more favourable light." In addition, they also said at trial judgement paragraph 297: "Regrettably, the Chamber also finds that in his evidence Lieutenant Colonel Panic sought to present aspects of his own role in a more favourable light and to avoid disclosing matters which could be construed as implicating Panic himself in criminal conduct." Isn't that precisely what you're doing now, avoiding disclosing matters that would implicate you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Do I strike you as that kind of person after everything we've done, after all the trials, all my evidence, the fact that I got in touch and appeared here today ?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: General, it's not for me to make any decisions about how you strike me. I'm simply putting to you how you struck the Trial Chamber. You see, General, it makes no sense at all that you as Chief of Staff --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: I have got the microphone. It's on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: General, it makes simply no sense that you as Chief of Staff would have had no knowledge about the withdrawal of troops within your zone of responsibility, particularly as you were taking over as commander the next day when Mrksic left. You must have known about what was going on, General, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: The next day at about 8.00, Mr. Mrksic left for Belgrade with a group of officers to see the federal secretary for National Defence. I went to the Vukovar barracks again with a group of officers. Soon after, this large group of journalists arrived, 120 of them. So in a formal sense, yes, I was standing-in that day for Commander Mrksic, but Mrksic was still alive. He was right there. He had communications equipment and was soon back from Belgrade. I'm not trying to defend myself. I am Mrksic's deputy --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: But, General, General, you appear to be suggesting that what was more important that day was your press conference, compared with the safety of nearly 200 prisoners of war that you yourself had raised concerns about their security the day before. Are you really suggesting you had made no inquiries as to what had happened to them?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: You see, the day before at the briefing Commander Mrksic gives an order for the 80th Brigade to be taking charge of the zone of responsibility. The 80th Brigade is a brigade whose zone of responsibility includes Ovcara, then as before. The Guards Brigade is now preparing to go back to Belgrade; that was one of the tasks. The other task was care of the civilians and their transport, and there was also the press conference. That was the task that I got from Mrksic. He said, "Welcome those people, greet them on my behalf, allow them to ask any questions they like, and allow them to go anywhere they like." That was the gist of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Wasn't part of the responsibility of Chief of Staff to ensure that the commander's orders were implemented on the ground; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes. Chief of Staff and everyone else was there to implement his orders at ground level.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: And part of his orders, according to you, was that the prisoners should be handed over to the government in order that trials should begin, according to you. So what steps did you take to ensure that was actually happening the next day, if that's what happened?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: On the 20th of November the hospital was evacuated. There was a selection procedure underway at the hospital. Some people were busy doing that. In parallel, there was a government meeting in progress on that day. You're asking me what I was doing. After the government meeting, I went back to the barracks --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: No, just pause --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: -- I briefed Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: No, just pause because I think you're not understanding my question. I'm referring to the 21st, the next day, forgive me if I didn't make that clear. The next day, on the 21st. Now, having had an order that these were to be tried, as you say, to be handed over, what steps did you take to make sure that had actually happened? Because that would have told you what was going on with these prisoners, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Well, if you allow, that's exactly what I'm trying to say. The government decision was implemented on the 20th. As early as the afternoon hours of the 20th these people were put up in the hangar at Ovcara. I left the government meeting, I went to the barracks, I briefed Mrksic. Having completed my business at the barracks, on my way back to the command post I took a turn and went to Ovcara. I was there outside the hangar at Ovcara. I saw the people there. I saw the commander of the unit providing their security. I saw the security detail deployed there. Upon my return, I spent no more than 15 minutes there, by the way, and then I went back to my command post. As soon as I was there, I briefed Commander Mrksic on everything I had been doing that day. I also told him, just to keep this brief, about the situation at Ovcara. So that was what I did and that was the 20th. On the 20th they were under the security regime of the 80th Brigade, just like the previous group who had left for Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Were there any meetings with the 80th Motorised Brigade on the morning of the 21st of November? Did you have contact with their commanders on the morning of the 21st of November?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: The 21st, I repeat, Mrksic and the delegation were getting ready to leave for Belgrade. Mr. Sljivancanin, Lieutenant-Colonel Maric, assistant for morale, and myself --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: -- were on our way to the barracks --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: -- there was no morning briefing on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: It was a very simple question. Did you have contact with commanders of the 80th Motorised Brigade on the morning of the 21st of November?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't and I don't know whether Mrksic did. Perhaps by phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: So you say that you remained completely ignorant that an entire group of soldiers had been removed and been withdrawn from the Ovcara farm? You had absolutely no idea that day or for several days later that the MPs had gone and they were no longer protecting the prisoners? That's your account, despite being deputy commander in charge of the zone of responsibility for that next day. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes. That day and generally speaking, I didn't go to Ovcara, nor did I contact the commander of the 80th Brigade on that day. He had been ordered to take charge of the entire responsibility zone of the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: So you're also suggesting by your answer --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat the last portion of his answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: There's a request to repeat the last portion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Panic, please repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 21st I was at the barracks. I did not meet the commander of the 80th Brigade. The commander of the 80th Brigade had taken charge of the area or taken over command of the area. The Guards Brigade was preparing to go back to the Belgrade garrison. We did not have any responsibility over that area anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Well, in the light of the finding of the Trial Chamber that it was indeed Mile Mrksic that ordered the withdrawal of the troops from Ovcara, what you're suggesting is that Mile Mrksic deliberately misled you and everyone else about issuing an order to withdraw. He deliberately failed to tell you an important fact relating to the command and the operation at the zone of responsibility over Operational Group South. Is that what you're suggesting in reality?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: No, that is not what I'm suggesting. What I'm suggesting is I've known Mrksic for a very long time and quite well. I cannot bring myself to believe that he could possibly have issued an order like that to anyone at all. An order like that could only possibly have come from the commander, but he certainly issued no such order in my presence. I was certainly not aware of that order, nor was anything like that ever mentioned in my presence or indeed during the conversation with Sljivancanin. Now, that is what I am suggesting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Rogers, I think your time is drawing closed. Do you have a new point to make? It seems that we are sort of repeating ourselves now?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think it's just fair to put to him that the -- because I'm not sure that he's following this point, that the effect of what he's saying is that the commander, given the finding that it was him who made the order, given that, the commander was in fact deliberately misleading him, the Chief of Staff, about something that was important in his zone of responsibility. And he couldn't hope for that not to be discovered because the command had gone to Vojnovic at the 80th. There was no hope that that could not be discovered. That's the point. And therefore there was no point in him doing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Judge Vaz, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I don't know if we can move forward, but I have a question for the witness. In the military line of command as it operated in your country, was it possible that Mr. Mrksic make a decision without consulting you, without consulting Mr. Sljivancanin, given an order that could be executed without your being told about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I looked at the Mrksic judgement, it said he had been convicted because he had ordered the withdrawal of the security detail from Ovcara. That was new to me. It seemed impossible to me. I know him as a commander, and he never told anyone that. Nevertheless, if you look at the command system in our army or any other army that works and operates based on the principles of subordination and singleness of command, no commander is duty-bound to inform all of his subordinates of all the orders that he issues. There is a certain honour that attaches to the role of commander and this is the price the commander pays. If the Trial Chamber established that this was something that he had done, he must have done this at his own initiative and perhaps with the knowledge of the last person in this chain executing the order, that means the security detail. An order like this could only have come from the commander and no one else but the commander within the chain of command. No subordinates would have been required to execute an order like that since executing it would have amounted to criminal responsibility. By way of conclusion, Mrksic could have taken that decision, could have issued that order without necessarily informing anyone, as you see. Did he actually do it? I don't know but I can't bring myself to believe that he did; however, it's possible. If I may, at Ovcara the commander of the 80th Brigade was directly subordinated to him. There are no mediators between the two, so that too would have been possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So you are saying that it is not impossible that Mrksic issued the command and he would have issued this command directed to the 80th Brigade without any inkling to the Chief of Staff, his own Chief of Staff, which would be yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that you have finished, Mr. Rogers, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, it would appear that I have, as Your Honours are telling me I have. It appears that I have. May I make one other point? I have one question related --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: -- to the 1st Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Simply this, General: What you're suggesting relating to the treatment of these prisoners was not only the -- relating to their hand-over, there was an order from the 1st Military District which was received in your command post in the early hours of the 20th of November at which -- required all the prisoners to be dealt with on an all-for-all exchange. Do you recall that order coming in? It's RP - forgive me - I think it's RP5.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, forgive me, I can't put my finger on it right now. Forgive me, it's RP11, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: It was an order of the 19th of November in which said this, I don't think you dispute this: "Competent organs shall continue working intensely on the implementation of the agreement on exchange of the arrested members of the SFRY OS and the captured members of the Ministry of the Interior and Croatian National Guards according to the all-for-all principle." And on the second page of that the date is the 20th of November and the time is 0045 hours in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, you have problems in finding the place?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No, I'd just like the witness to have the document because --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yeah, it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It would be fair to him to at least know what document we're dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: It's RP --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: It's RP11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: He has a binder. It's in Sanction as well at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: I think you have the original order. And you'll see the first paragraph dealing with the all-for-all principle.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: And the second page you see the stamp, if you turn it over you'll see the stamp, which shows when it was received --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: -- in the early hours of the morning of the 20th of November.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Having received that, was that an order you were aware of on the 20th of November, the all-for-all principle order from the 1st Military District?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. That's the way things were done. And that first group had gone to Mitrovica on the basis of that principle. As for the second group, what followed was the government decision because they had already started functioning as the authority there. They had decided that they would try them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: So there was already a breach of the order of the 1st Military District that you were tolerating; is that right? These prisoners were supposed to be exchanged all-for-all, not tried.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Well, that's the way things were supposed to happen up until then, and then it was on the 20th that an exception was made. A government decision was made and accepted by Commander Mrksic, but according to the same methods, they were put up at the hangar in Ovcara and they were secured by the same unit like the previous group that had been taken to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: So you agree that the way these prisoners were handled was in breach of the order of the 1st Military District and you knew about that at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: As I went to the government session, I had the position of my commander, and that is the position that I appeared with at that meeting. They passed certain conclusions and I made my commander aware of them. He accepted that. And I was just one of the persons implementing this. I was not the creator of that decision and it was not my idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Final question: So you were implementing the order in direct contravention of the order of the 1st Military District; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: That's my last question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. There was no contravention as far as my execution of tasks was concerned. It was -- it's not the commander of the 1st District that issues tasks to me; it is my commander, Colonel Mrksic, who gives me tasks and issues orders to me. Now, whether he had violated something or whether someone had approved of the decision that he had made, well I can assume that he had to ask someone about that decision because that is a major decision, it is a big decision. It is a government decision, the commander accepts it, and they are probably in contact, Mrksic with his superiors. But at that point in time, he is my superior. I just carried out the tasks that he had given me, that is to say to attend the session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Panic. Here we are. We are finished with cross-examination of Panic by the Prosecutor. We will now have a 20-minute break. We will resume exactly at 12.35 and we will then have re-examination of Panic by the counsel of Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please be seated. Next time we reconvene, I would be grateful if everybody would be waiting for the Bench, not vice versa. Now, the counsel for Mr. Sljivancanin will now conduct a re-examination of Panic for 15 minutes, followed by 15 minutes of summary arguments concerning Mr. Panic's testimony; and finally, the Prosecution will have summary arguments for 15 minutes. And I would be grateful if everybody would stick to the timetable. Mr. Bourgon, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just found the page I was missing. Sorry. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Welcome back, Mr. Panic. I only have a few questions for you in re-examination this morning. My first question relates to a question that was put to you by my colleague at page 42, lines 22 to 25. At that moment my colleague was drawing your attention on the statement which you provided to the Sljivancanin Defence on 8 October. So you understand what statement I'm talking about, do you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, my colleague suggested to you that when you drafted that statement you were supposed to brief to the fullest everything that happened during the conversation between Mrksic and Sljivancanin on that night. What I would like to know from you is: What was your understanding at the moment you are drafting this statement were you supposed to give a full account of that conversation or were you supposed to give or to talk about the basic things that happened during that conversation?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: That statement consists of two handwritten pages only. There are just a few lines on the third page. That statement could not include each and every little detail. I have already responded to that question here in part. Had I described all the details involved, I would have needed 20 pages. That was my understanding and that is what I did; namely, in the statement I just put down the basic facts so that the Defence could use that, if it is valid, for these proceedings. That is how I understood the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Panic. Now, in cross-examination my colleague established - and of course that was obvious - that in this statement you did not mention anything about the hospital, but today you spoke about the hospital. So my question is the following. When I look at your statement I see that you mention that the Guards Brigade was redeploying to Belgrade, that the 80th Motorised Brigade was about to take-over responsibility for the area, and you also spoke about a press conference. Is there any reasons why you mentioned these three things and not the hospital issue or other things?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Well, I outlined the most important tasks and what pressured me the most, what I was supposed to carry out during the course of the day. That is why I outlined these main tasks that our command dealt with and the subordinate units too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now during your examination-in-chief you said that you may have missed some words of what was said between Mrksic and Sljivancanin, and my colleague established that again in cross-examination with you. Now, my question is: To the best of your recollection, General Panic, did you miss any topics that were discussed during that conversation?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Well, to the best of my recollection and looking at the documents, trying to refresh my memory, I did not miss the main topics of the conversation. It is possible that something unimportant may have slipped by after all this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, I'd like to follow-up on a question which was put to you by His Excellency Judge Guney, and I think it is a very important question. The question was: Why did Mrksic not mention the order to withdraw to you or to -- I think he mentioned the exact question to the -- to his security officer. And you provided an answer. Now, I'd like in order for us to fully understand the answer that you give, can you expand on the relationship which exists or which existed, sorry, between Mrksic and Sljivancanin at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the briefest possible terms, the relations between Mrksic and Sljivancanin were based on the principle of subordination and mutual respect. However, Mrksic was the commander who was stern, well-balanced, and he didn't let people very close to him. In conclusion, their relations were proper and soldierly. Since Sljivancanin is also security officer, I can give you a view of my very own, and I was a commander as well. Commanders often do not like to have security officers close to them for reasons known to them. They thought that sometimes they dealt with questions that go beyond the scope of their duty and service.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, it was established on your -- during your testimony today that - and you spoke about that in cross-examination - the consequences of the withdrawal of the military police from Ovcara. So when we consider that relationship between Mrksic and Sljivancanin, who is of course the chief of security, based on your vast military experience would you expect a commander who has just given an order which has dreadful consequences for prisoners of war to tell what he just did to a security officer?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's a -- it's a leading question. Would he expect that to happen suggests the answer in it. And in any event, I'm not sure what speculations are helpful in this regard from this witness, the motives for individuals to act are not really an issue here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Still I think it would be interesting for us to hear an answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If Mrksic as commander would decide to take such a course, namely, to order the withdrawal of the security detail from Ovcara and thus directly endanger the safety and lives of people, it is not logical if he had done that or if he would have done that that he'd discuss that with a security officer because the duties of the security officer include working against such things that involve criminal liability. So that very instant he could have filed criminal -- a criminal complaint against him, not only the security officer but any other officer, any other officer could react to that. And even if he had made such a decision, he did not communicate it to anyone, least of all to the security officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now I move to the 21st of November, which was covered in cross-examination. You mentioned that you were involved in the press conference --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: You are aware of the time constraints.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I have five minutes left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Well, I think that you already had 15, didn't you, since you started?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I just started, Mr. President. I have two more -- three more questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, beside the press conference, what other activities, briefly, were you involved in yourself on the 21st of November?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: I personally, together with a group of officers, including Major Sljivancanin, Lieutenant-Colonel Maric, went to the barracks in relation to the press conference, welcoming the journalists, that is, and the press conference itself. My other task that I had not been prepared for and that I had not expected was that the commander sent me during the implementation of the previous task, he actually telephoned me and sent me to the government session. I attended the government session. I came back to barracks --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sorry, General, we're talking the 21st of November.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Oh, the 21st, sorry, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You mentioned you were involved in a press conference in the morning. What else were you involved in on that day?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, sorry. After the press conference I went back to carrying out my tasks related to the return of the brigade to the Belgrade garrison. Then a very, very large number of civilians started coming back from the border, convoys that were not accepted by anyone, that nobody would take. There were lots of them. Then also units from combat deployment were supposed to be returned slowly to normal life, which is very pain-staking. We had spent about two months in war conditions. Winter had set in and there were many, many problems that we were resolving in the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. And my last question is the following: Which unit was responsible for the area and the prisoners of war at Ovcara on the 21st of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: On the 21st of November, 1991, the area of responsibility that includes Ovcara and the hangar where these suspects were was under the responsibility of the 80th Brigade, that is to say that it was the 80th Brigade that had this area of responsibility that included Ovcara, Negrovac, Grabovo, and they had already taken over the area of responsibility that had previously been held by the Guards Brigade. Let me note that they had had that zone or area earlier on as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Now you will have 15 minutes of summary arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Is the witness remaining in the room for these arguments?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. I think that we can thank -- unless there is -- no. I think we can thank the witness, but he would remain available should we need him in the course of the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm willing to begin now. I'm just saying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Panic, thank you for your testimony. You are excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Until ten past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will have the honour of addressing the Appeals Chamber concerning the testimony of Witness Panic, whom we just heard. In accordance with the Scheduling Order, I only have 15 minutes, so I will go straight to the point. The purpose of hearing Witness Panic this morning was to assess the evidentiary value and relevance of his testimony. Now, we must say that we understand the concerns of Judge Pocar expressed in his dissenting opinion regarding this hearing today. As Defence counsel, we're always the first to say we want the Statute to be abided strictly. However, we're grateful, Mr. President, for being given this opportunity to assess the probative value of the evidence provided by Witness Panic. In fact, we take the view, as expressed in our application for review, that calling Miodrag Panic to testify before the Appeals Chamber this morning about this proposed new fact was not only justified, it was absolutely necessary, bearing in mind the exceptional circumstances of this case. Now, we're in a position now to say now that we've heard him mission accomplished, Mr. President. The purpose of hearing Witness Panic has been achieved. We now know beyond any doubt that Miodrag Panic was present when Sljivancanin had this short conversation with Commander Mrksic in the evening of 20 November 1991. We know that Panic heard a conversation. And we know that during this conversation Mrksic did not tell Sljivancanin that he had withdrawn the MPs from guarding the prisoners at Ovcara. General Panic made it clear during his testimony that if anything of the kind had been mentioned by Mile Mrksic during that conversation, he could not have missed it, as he said, and he would have immediately reacted. Why? Because he said this would have been a change of plan which Panic knew would have endangered the safety of the prisoners being held at Ovcara. Now, he would have reacted about the order itself, which would have been the change of plan, but he said, "I would also have reacted because I should have been informed as well as others in the command." That's what he said. He said: Commander - and I don't have to repeat his words. Now, that was necessary also for the planning purposes. Now, based on the testimony of Panic, there are no reasons to doubt that the conversation between Sljivancanin and Mrksic at the OG South command did not include any reference to the withdrawal of the MPs guarding the prisoners at Ovcara. Now, whereas before there is no direct evidence of what was said during that conversation, other of course than for the testimony of Sljivancanin - and it's important to note when we speak about Sljivancanin that the question was not -- never even put to him: Hey, Sljivancanin, did the commander inform of you this order? Never. Never by Mrksic, never by the Prosecution, never by Mr. Lukic, never by the Judges. So we now have a source of direct evidence, and that's the direct evidence we've heard this morning. And we say, Mr. President, it must be attributed full probative value. Now, of course I look at Witness Panic this morning. At times he was hesitant. We never know really if it's the translation that he's waiting for or if he's thinking about his answer. But the key question that the Appeals Chamber must ask or answer this morning: Is General Panic a liar? Is -- did General Panic fabricate the evidence that he put before the Chamber this morning? It is our submission, Mr. President - and there can be no doubt that the answer to both questions - is a straightforward no. So what can we conclude from his testimony? Well, I can't list everything that we can conclude, but let me try to get to the most important and relevant issues. Panic is a professional military army officer. The Appeals Chamber knows how successful he was. He ended up as a two-star general. And while watching the appeals judgement on the internet, something mystified him. Maybe I'm putting -- I'm adding a bit of emotion here. But he said he was surprised by what he heard. He said he tried to look. Is that really what I heard? And until that night when his daughter came and with the help of his daughter, he checked on the internet, he found a summary, and he says: Almighty God, what I heard is true. But I know that this is not true. What do I do about it? Well, he didn't sleep that night, and he said so. What he did next, he picked up the phone and he called Mr. Lukic. Why? Because he had to say that that conversation he could not accept that a man would go down. He said: Is this why Sljivancanin was convicted? So because of that he calls. And he says what he discussed with Mr. Lukic and what Mr. Lukic told him to do. So now we know the origin of the new fact. We know where and why he's here this morning. The next thing, Mr. President, when Panic testified before the Trial Chamber in this case, it was significant that the Trial Chamber found him to be a credible witness. It is true that in some respect my colleague raised a few issues here, where the Chamber did not fully accept his testimony, but after hearing him this morning we have a better understanding of these issues for -- the issues for which the Trial Chamber maybe did not accept fully his testimony. But what's important is that those issues for which the Trial Chamber did not accept fully his testimony are not related to that conversation he was here to talk about this morning. Thirdly, Mr. President, it's very important to note that the Prosecution today - of course they tried to undermine the credibility of the witness, that's their job, I didn't expect anything else - but at trial they relied on this testimony during their final brief and their final arguments. They relied on this testimony, they believed him, and today they're saying it's not possible what he's saying. When Mrksic raised a ground of appeal saying that Panic was not a credible witness, in response they said that ground of appeal must be dismissed. The Chamber correctly assessed the credibility of Panic. Now, fourthly, the Appeals Chamber has already had the opportunity when it dismissed the ground of appeal raised by Mrksic concerning the credibility of Panic to assess his credibility. It is our respectful submission, Mr. President, this morning that after you've -- now that you've heard him, you should be even more convinced that he's a credible witness. The Appeals Chamber should know by now that the purpose of his testimony has been -- has not been to protect himself or else he would not be here this morning, as he said. Fifthly, the fact that Panic provided statements to any party in this case is also very important. He was ready to testify for anyone; he said so, whether the Prosecution, whether the Defence, whether Belgrade, whether The Hague. His purpose has always been to contribute to the establishment of the truth. Sixthly, even though - and that's the crux here - even though he was surprised by the finding of the Trial Chamber that Mrksic is the one who issued the order, he's surprised by that, but he explained that. He explained that at trial before the finding and he explained it now after the finding. I know Mrksic, "dobar komandant," he's not the type of guy who's going to give an order like that. But he did not hesitate to say at the same time, and he said it again today, it can only have come from the commander. Now, that's critical, Mr. President. Seventhly, the fact that Panic was never asked by anyone about the contents of the conversation, even though it had been established way from the beginning that he was present when the conversation took place, that's also an important conversation, and we say that is also revealing today as to why he's here. Moving on, Mr. President, I'd like to address one very important issue, and I'm almost done. As you can see from his testimony this morning, his recollection of the contents of the conversation which he heard is not exactly the same as that of Sljivancanin. Well, I'll tell you, Mr. President, that's absolutely normal. No two people can report a conversation in which they were involved or in which they heard 19 years ago and report that in the exact same terms or the exact same words. Did he miss any topics? Did he miss any important issue? Even the issue that my colleague raised about the exchange of the prisoners, that topic was covered by what he recalls from that conversation. But the crux of the matter, Mr. President, is that Witness Panic is absolutely certain that Mrksic did not make any reference during that conversation to the withdrawal of the MPs, and he's also 100 per cent certain that he could not have missed if it had been said by Mrksic. He explained what he would have done in such circumstances. Now, the last thing I'd like to raise here is, of course the Prosecution tried at the end to say it's not possible that Mrksic gave this order without telling him. Well, firstly, the witness said yes it is possible. It doesn't come off, but it is possible. The commander is not duty-bound to tell everything that he does and every order he issues. But the witness candidly and honestly said: I should have been informed, because that's the normal practice. Yes, the normal practice is for the Chief of Staff to be informed, but that's the normal practice. There is no obligation for Mrksic to inform everybody. Now, that's not the issue here. The issue is there's a reason why Mrksic would not say that during that conversation, many reasons, and we went through that during his testimony. And the other reason is we now know that there was a -- there was a direct line, as he mentioned today, between Mrksic and Vojnovic. So there are plenty of issues that -- question marks as to exactly how this happened, but that doesn't change anything from the judgement of the Trial Chamber that Mrksic issued the order. He accepts that. It surprises him but he accepts it. But he says, I still have trouble living with that today. Now, the Prosecution, we say, did not put that question, whether to him, whether to Sljivancanin, whether to anybody. It's too late now to say: Come on, Mr. Chief of Staff, you knew about that order, didn't you? Why did the Prosecution not say that at trial? They didn't say that at trial. They used his testimony. Last thing, Mr. President, simply that - and this refers to the applicable burden of proof in such -- in the cases that we find ourselves now. It is our submission that we need not prove the proposed new fact beyond a reasonable doubt for our review application to be successful. Honestly, I haven't found anything on the record that says what is the applicable burden of proof. But we say - and it is our submission - that all that is required is that we prove the fact sufficiently to raise a doubt regarding the inference which was adopted by the Appeals Chamber at paragraph 62, in which case we say the judgement cannot stand. But nonetheless, even if you put -- brush aside completely our arguments and if you don't accept our arguments, it doesn't matter. If the Appeals Chamber was to hold that the new fact must be proved beyond a reasonable doubt, it is our submission that we have achieved this standard through the testimony of General Panic this morning. And that is why, Mr. President, we submit that Mrksic did not tell Sljivancanin in the evening of 20 November 1991 when they met at that OG South command during a very specific conversation which forms the basis of the judgement, Mrksic never said to Sljivancanin that he had withdrawn the MPs guarding the prisoners at Ovcara. This is what stems from the testimony of Witness Panic. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Mr. Rogers, 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, in our respectful submission, the evidential value of this witness's testimony in this particular case and these particular circumstances is of no value in our submission, and that is because he is not reasonably capable of belief in relation to these matters. The knowledge of the order to withdraw does on his own admission implicate him, implicate him in probable criminal or, in this case, actual criminal activity. He cannot admit, as he said, to it being said because, in our submission, it would fix him with knowledge and therefore would have required him, as he accepted, to act. And indeed Your Honours will recall he was really rather forthright about what he said he would have had to have done if he had been made aware of those materials and those facts relating to the withdrawal. Whenever he is implicated in the consequences or in relation to criminal activity, he has minimised his role, as was found by the Trial Chamber, he has lied, and he has misled. We stand by the Trial Chamber's credibility findings because they were nuanced, they were sensible, and they were sensitive to the particular demands of the case, and they had the opportunity over four days to hear General Panic give evidence, and they very carefully identified the areas of his testimony that were not reliable. Those areas of his testimony that were not reliable were those areas in which he was implicated himself. The Chamber made a number of really very nuanced findings relating to him. They found him to be a liar. They didn't use the word "liar," but in our submission that is what they held. At trial judgement paragraph 307 they found that the Chamber was unable to accept his explanation as to why he was at Ovcara. "It is entirely lacking in credibility that he believed that trials of prisoners could be in progress at Ovcara. There was manifestly no time for this to have been implemented, even if there had been the necessary skilled investigators ..." et cetera. And they went on to make a finding as to why he was there. "In the Chamber's finding his presence at Ovcara was to assess the position and to report to Mile Mrksic." Finding someone to be entirely lacking in credibility on a point that they testified about is clearly to hold them to have told lies about it. Furthermore, they held at paragraph 585 of the judgement: "In his evidence about the meeting, Lieutenant-Colonel Panic sought to say that from the debate at the meeting it appeared that the SAO 'government' planned to put the war criminals on trial. While he indicated he believed this to be their intention, when he conveyed Mile Mrksic's position, the Chamber is quite unable to accept the honesty of this aspect of his evidence. It was obviously self-serving, and also an attempt to put the JNA and Mile Mrksic in a more favourable light." In the same way, in our submission, his distancing himself from this conversation to the extent that he has to say nothing was said about the order to withdraw is obviously self-serving and an attempt to put Sljivancanin in a more favourable light. And clearly it's something that he has done before and would be prepared to do again. The Chamber went on at trial judgement 297: "Regrettably, the Chamber also finds that in his evidence Lieutenant-Colonel Panic sought to present aspects of his own role in a more favourable light and to avoid disclosing matters which could be construed as implicating Panic himself in criminal conduct." Precisely the point here.
