The Chamber found him in addition at -- to be less than frank about his role, as it was once famously suggested in the Spycatcher trial in the United Kingdom in 1986, the phrase "he was economical with the truth" was used. At paragraph 297 the Chamber said this: "The Chamber is persuaded that the evidence of Lieutenant-Colonel Panic underplays the full extent of his knowledge of the situation at the barracks that morning." It went on: "When questioned about this aspect, it was the evidence of Lieutenant-Colonel Panic that there was no threat to the prisoners on the bus as all security measures had been taken, and he appeared to deny seeing any mistreatment of prisoners at the barracks that day. In the Chamber's finding, the role of Lieutenant-Colonel Panic in conveying the instructions from Mile Mrksic for the meeting and his own role at the meeting," note that, I underscore that, and his own role at the meeting, "provide reason for Lieutenant-Colonel Panic not to be fully frank and honest about the events he saw at the barracks concerning the convoy of prisoners of war." It went on at trial judgement 308: "... while the Chamber had the clear impression of Lieutenant-Colonel Panic as he gave his evidence, that the witness was not being frank when speaking of his own knowledge of the mistreatment of the prisoners of war that day, so as to minimise the truth in that respect ...," trial judgement 308. And at trial judgement 262: "The Chamber also recognises that Lieutenant-Colonel Panic may have seen more of the mistreatment of the prisoners of war outside the hangar than he acknowledged in his evidence in which event his evidence in this respect would not have been entirely frank, no doubt out of self interest." And if that wasn't enough to dispose of him in relation to these areas in relation to his credibility, they went on to deal with other ways in which the witness was prepared to amend or alter or be influenced in his testimony. They said this: "In" -- this is at trial judgement 396 and it related to a conflict between what Colonel Panic had said in his OTP witness statement relating to the role of Veselin Sljivancanin and what he subsequently testified about. And they said this: "In this respect, the Chamber accepts the honesty and correctness of the account of Mile Mrksic's statement to the briefing, given by Lieutenant-Colonel Panic in a written statement he gave to the Prosecution investigators. The Chamber does so after careful consideration of the course of evidence of Lieutenant-Colonel Panic," evidence of course given under oath, "in which he sought to qualify the effect of his prior statement. When this was more fully explored with Lieutenant-Colonel Panic, however, it became clear in the view of the Chamber that his evidence sought to accommodate what he described as documents, with which he had been familiarised, and which he said helped him realise that in his statement he had ascribed to Veselin Sljivancanin certain powers which he did not have at the relevant time." Your Honours, I pause there to recall the -- a number of times during testimony today in which Colonel Panic -- General Panic as he now -- he's retired, referred to his recollection and refreshing his memory from other documents and materials that he was provided with. And I remind the Chamber that he was provided with the statements of Sljivancanin prior to testimony -- prior to this testimony. So relevant parts of that testimony were read to him to assist him. "From his evidence," they went on, "as with a number of other JNA former JNA witnesses, it appears that attempts were made to persuade Lieutenant-Colonel Panic that, in the light of the military rules applicable at the time, his recollection of the words of Mile Mrksic about Veselin Sljivancanin was erroneous." So again he's been influenced. Further they held at trial judgement 261: "The evidence of Lieutenant-Colonel Panic and some others, such as P014, as to the timing of events that afternoon, appeared to the Chamber to be based substantially on genuine attempts to rationalise the events of the afternoon rather than precise recollection." Your Honours, in our submission, all of those factors may well be and in our submission are at play in the evidence given by General Panic today. He appears to be one of the few individuals capable of improving his memory over 19 years, as opposed for it to be degenerating over 19 years. Each time he comes to recall these events or at least record them, it appears they improve rather than get worse. More memories come forward than one might otherwise expect. Is that because he is genuinely attempting to rationalise events that were going on? Is it because they implicate him and he has to distance himself from them? Is it that the true passage of time may well be taking its toll and that he now misremembers, does not accurately recall what was said? And Your Honours will have in mind the number of points that were made during the course of the hearing relating to the content of what he said when he was making his statement, the content of what he said in evidence, and the fact that new material was put to him during the course of the hearing which he then accommodated into his evidence. At the end of the day, is he reasonably capable of belief in the background that you have relating to the findings about credibility made by him and your own impressions having heard him today? That's before one even takes into account the absurdity of a situation in our submission where the Chief of Staff of an operational group appears to be wholly in the dark about what was going on with 200 prisoners that he, the very day before, had twice reported on to Mrksic relating to their care, custody, and safety. Was he really so consumed with the press conference the next day that all thought of the 200 prisoners, for which he had legitimate, he says, security concerns - and bearing in mind he's underplayed his role according to the Chamber, so his actual knowledge may be much greater - is it really realistic that he would have done nothing and that the first ever knew about what had happened was days later? It's simply inconceivable. It's inconceivable that he did not hear, as Your Honours found to be the case, that during the course of that conversation the order to withdraw was communicated to Sljivancanin, especially when we know that the purpose of Sljivancanin's attendance that day at the barracks -- sorry, at the command post was to report, in our submission, was to inform his commander about what he'd done, receive instructions, is it really realistic given that the Chamber found he was in charge of the evacuation that that conversation would not have been had and that information not imparted to Mr. Sljivancanin in the presence of Mr. Panic? It's inconceivable in a functioning chain of command, in a disciplined organisation such as the Guards Brigade, and Your Honours will recall Panic's evidence about that, about how they were an elite unit, that this chain of command would so catastrophically break down in the way that it did. For all those reasons, Your Honours, the evidence of General Panic in relation to these matters is not credible, it is not reasonably capable of belief, and we invite you to disregard it and dismiss this application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rogers, for your argument. We will now have a one-hour break. So we will meet here at 2.25. And this afternoon we will hear testimony -- we will hear arguments on whether Panic's testimony constitutes a new fact. So we will now stand adjourned for one hour. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.25 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Before we start this afternoon's programme, let me note that all documents referred to during the hearing today and not already part of the record will be considered annexes to the party's motion, that will make it simple. I take it no objection to that. Now, we will turn to the final stage of our proceedings today, arguments on whether Panic testimony constitutes a new fact. Mr. Bourgon, you will be arguing now or Mr. Lukic? Mr. Bourgon, you will have 45 minutes, then Mr. Rogers -- or I see Ms. Brady there, Ms. Brady, 45 minutes. And then, Mr. Bourgon, you will have the final 15 minutes reply. Okay, so please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. And thank you very much. Good afternoon to the Judges. And good afternoon to my colleagues from the Prosecution. Pursuant to the Scheduling Order, Mr. President, on behalf of Mr. Sljivancanin I have the honour of addressing the Appeals Chamber for the next 45 minutes on one single issue, and that is whether the testimony of Witness Panic heard this morning constitutes a new fact. Our legal arguments stricto sensu on this issue are included, as you know, Mr. President, in our application for review and even more so in our reply to the Prosecution's response. I do not intend to repeat these arguments one by one. I'm sure you've had the chance to read those and I will focus on some specific issues. What I really want to do this afternoon is to convince you that the new information provided by Witness Panic, first in his statement provided to us in October 2009, that was at the time, Mr. President, you will recall that we filed our motion for reconsideration in which we referred to Panic and that's why we had chosen that date for him to make his statement; but also during his testimony this morning. That this information constitutes a new fact pursuant to the applicable law and the jurisprudence of the Appeals Chamber on this issue. I intend to do so by drawing your attention on four different aspects or ways of considering the new evidence provided by Witness Panic which all lead to the same conclusion. The fact that Miodrag Panic heard the conversation between Sljivancanin and his commander, that is, in the evening of 20 November 1991, that is, the conversation when Sljivancanin returned to the Operational Group South sometimes after 8.00, or 8.00 p.m. for those of us who are not military, is a new fact which makes it necessary for the Appeals Chamber to review its judgement and to reinstate the acquittal of Mr. Sljivancanin which was pronounced at trial after hearing all the evidence in this case, that is, more than 90 witnesses over a period of more than 18 months. In other words, Mr. President, the issue this afternoon is strictly limited to the first of four criteria which must be fulfilled for the Appeals Chamber to review its own judgement. And of course our position is clear. There can be no doubt that the testimony of Witness Panic fully meets the requirements of this criteria. My arguments this afternoon will be divided into four distinct topics. I will first address the new fact pursuant to the plain meaning of the words found in Article 26 of the Statute and Rules 119, 120; secondly, I will demonstrate how and for what reasons the testimony of Panic meets the new fact test developed in the jurisprudence of the Appeals Chamber; thirdly, I will expose why the new information provided by Witness Panic, which of course can clearly be distinguished from the alleged new facts which form the basis of previous applications for review, and that's another reason why it does constitute a new fact; fourthly, and finally, I will address the testimony of Witness Panic pursuant to what I call the forest test. In other words, I will make it obvious to you, Mr. President, that although the Prosecution may ask you to look at all the trees in the world, they cannot prevent you from seeing the forest. Before I move to my first argument, there's of course an additional issue which was raised in the Scheduling Order which I must address as a preliminary matter, namely, the exceptional circumstances --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpreters. It's been a while since I was in court and I'm trying to meet my 45-minute dead-line. So before I move on, that's one issue I wish to raise which was in the Scheduling Order, and that is the exceptional circumstances of this case because we believe that this is directly related to the issue whether it does constitute a new fact or not. The exceptional circumstances of this case were described in our application for review at paragraphs 30 to 38, but let me summarise briefly. The reversal of Sljivancanin's acquittal for murder and his conviction on appeal rest on a single inference because the Appeals Chamber confirmed that there is no direct evidence that Sljivancanin was informed of the withdrawal in the course of his meeting with Mrksic. And the Appeals Chamber added Mrksic and Panic, and that was at paragraph 62. Now, of course we now know, Mr. President, that Sljivancanin had a meeting with Mrksic in the presence of Panic and not with Mrksic and Panic, but I will return to this later because this is all together different. As we heard this morning Witness Panic, he said he heard the conversation between Sljivancanin and his commander, during which Mrksic did not inform Sljivancanin of the withdrawal. Thus, Mr. President, if you attach probative value to the witness -- to the testimony of Witness Panic, quite simply the inference drawn by the Appeals Chamber is nullified, considering that it can no longer be said that Mrksic must have told Sljivancanin about the withdrawal. Consequently, without this watershed inference which brought everything else thereafter, the Sljivancanin's conviction for murder on appeal cannot stand. No new fact could be more decisive, Mr. President. To make myself clear let me use an example. Suppose Sljivancanin had been found guilty of aiding and abetting the murder of Mr. Smith, and the following week it was established that Mr. Smith was never murdered and that he is well alive. Could Sljivancanin's conviction stand? Now, I'm not referring, Mr. President, to the exact same scenario which you raised in your separate opinion in the Niyitegeka decision on request for review of 6 March, 2007, but I will come to that topic later. What we say, Mr. President, is that the present case falls in the exact same category, which is why it is exceptional. Panic said -- as established by Panic, Mrksic did not inform Sljivancanin of the withdrawal, therefore the Appeals Chamber inference is nullified by his testimony, which is something that was not known before. Accordingly, the conviction for murder cannot stand. In our respectful opinion, Mr. President, there is a direct relationship between the decisive character of the evidence provided by General Panic and whether it constitutes a new fact. Just as Sljivancanin could not have been convicted for the murder of Mr. Smith if there was evidence that he was alive, his conviction in the present case would not have been possible if the evidence of the new fact provided by Panic, that is, of course, that Mrksic did not inform Sljivancanin of the withdrawal, had been available. But that information was not available to the Appeals Chamber. In both instances, the example of Mr. Smith or the present case, the information which came to light must constitute a new fact pursuant to Article 26 of the Statute which was designed specifically to address such cases. This brings me to the first of my four arguments, namely, the plain meaning of the word "new" in Article 26 of the Statute and Rules 119 and 120. Pursuant to the new oxford American dictionary: "Something new is nothing more than something not existing before, something discovered now for the first time." Applying this definition to Article 26 of the Statute and Rules 119 and 120, it follows that a new fact is no more than a fact which did not exist or was not established at the time of the proceedings before a Trial Chamber or the Appeals Chamber and which has been discovered for the first time thereafter. Clearly, Mr. President, a tough word for a frenchman, this teleological interpretation of the word "new" applies to the evidence provided by Witness Panic this morning. Once again, the acquittal of Sljivancanin for murder was reversed on appeal, as we know, without any possibility of a further appeal. But the Appeals Chamber confirmed there was no direct evidence that Sljivancanin was informed of the withdrawal in the course of his meeting with Mrksic. Bearing in mind that the evidence provided by General Panic this morning constitutes a source of direct evidence as to what was said during this conversation, it is thus evident that this information did not exist or, in other words, was not known or was not established at the time of the proceedings before the Appeals Chamber. It therefore constitutes a new fact. Another way to look at this is to consider that the dissenting opinion of Judge Vaz appended to the Appeals Chamber judgement. Judge Vaz said the following at page 172, paragraph 4, I quote: "There is no clear evidence cited in support of the Appeals Chamber's conclusion that Mrksic must have told Sljivancanin that he had withdrawn the JNA protection. To the contrary, this crucial conclusion, which must be the only reasonable one, appears to be solely based on Sljivancanin's testimony that he inquired about further tasks and duties, although there is no evidence as to what Mrksic actually responded to that inquiry." Taking into account that the evidence offered by Panic establishes what was said during the Mrksic/Sljivancanin conversation, the only reasonable conclusion is that his evidence did not exist, this new information did not exist at the time of the proceedings before the Appeals Chamber and that it does constitute a new fact. Moving on to my second argument this afternoon. It is our submission, Mr. President, that applying the definition of new fact as developed in the case law of the Appeals Chamber yields the same conclusion; that is, the evidence offered by Miodrag Panic indeed constitutes a new fact. Pursuant to the jurisprudence of the Appeals Chamber, the key question before a Chamber in determining whether a fact proffered in a review proceeding is actually new is whether the fact raised by the new evidentiary information was at issue during the trial or appeal proceedings, that was at Blaskic review applications decision paragraphs 15 and 40. Moreover, the Appeals Chamber has further interpreted this requirement, holding that this means - that's the fact of being an issue - this means that it must not have been amongst the factors that the deciding body could have taken into account in reaching its verdict. That was Tadic, paragraph 25; Blaskic, paragraph 14; Rutaganda, paragraph 9. These are all, of course, review application decisions. In other words, what is relevant is whether the deciding body, the Appeals Chamber in this case, knew about the fact or not in arriving at the decision, Tadic, paragraph 25; Rutaganda, paragraph 9. Applying this test to the new information provided by General Panic in his testimony this morning, we can only conclude that his evidence constitutes a new fact. How so? Well, firstly the Panic new fact was clearly identified in our application for review as well as in our reply to the Prosecution response. And we have explained why the Panic new fact was not in issue both at trial and on appeal. I will not repeat these arguments. Secondly, the crux of the matter pursuant to the test developed by the Appeals Chamber is, and I quote, "the requirement for the moving party," that is us, "to show that the Chamber did not know about the fact in reaching its decision." In the present case, what was known to the Appeals Chamber? Well, it was known, inter alia, that Sljivancanin did not attend the daily briefing in the evening of 20 November. It was known that Sljivancanin was not involved in the transmission of the withdrawal order. It was known that Sljivancanin returned to the Operational Group South command shortly after 2000 hours on 20 November. It was also known to the Appeals Chamber that upon arriving at the command, Sljivancanin had a short conversation with his commander. And it was also known to the Appeals Chamber that Panic was present during this conversation. However, what is most significant here is that the Appeals Chamber did not know that Panic heard the conversation and, even more importantly, that Mrksic did not tell Sljivancanin during this conversation anything about the withdrawal. On what basis can we affirm this, Mr. President? Well, on the following. Firstly, when Sljivancanin testified and mentioned the presence of Panic during his conversation with Mrksic, he's the one who brought it up, he was testifying in his own defence and he brought it up. When that took place, no one asked him whether Panic was a party to the conversation; if Panic was a party to the conversation, what did Panic say during this conversation; and if Panic was not a party to the conversation, whether Panic could hear the conversation. None of this was asked to Sljivancanin. Secondly, on the basis that when Panic took the stand after the testimony of Sljivancanin and confirmed that he was present at the Operational Group South command when Sljivancanin returned in the evening of 20 November and had a conversation with his commander, you had Panic right there on the stand. Nobody asked him: Were you a party to that conversation, General? That was not asked. If you were a party, what did you say during the conversation? Not a question about that. If he was not a party, could you hear the conversation, General? Not a word about that. I make a short pause here, Mr. President, just to say that it is very significant that this morning the Prosecution asked the Appeals Chamber to apply specific findings on credibility drawn by the Trial Chamber, whereas to apply this to questions that were never put to Panic. Now, that's quite incredible, but I move on. Thirdly, also on the basis that a number of other witnesses appeared which could have been asked if Panic heard and what Panic heard or what was said. No questions were asked to any other witness. Now, this conclusion is supported by the Trial Chamber's finding at paragraph 389. The Trial Chamber found Lieutenant-Colonel Panic was there. No comments were made by the Trial Chamber, no information was provided regarding what Panic could have said, could have heard or said during this conversation. Of course, the Trial Chamber was not as surprised, because as mentioned by the Trial Chamber in footnote 1553, it is based solely on the testimony of Sljivancanin and nothing else. Now, even though the Appeals Chamber stated at paragraph 61 that there is no evidence that Sljivancanin was informed of the withdrawal in the course of his meeting with Mrksic and Panic, which appears to be a different finding on its face, we now know based on the accurate interpretation in English of Sljivancanin's testimony in B/C/S, that Sljivancanin really had a conversation with his commander in the presence of Panic, exactly as the Trial Chamber found. I take this, Mr. President, from the fact that during his testimony Sljivancanin really said: I wanted to tell, and not: I wanted to tell them. That is transcript 13987, lines 5 to 7. And also because he really said "I called in to Colonel Mrksic ," pause, and "I briefly informed him" and not "I informed them ." Transcript 13665, lines 14 to 18. Considering, Mr. President, that the Appeals Chamber quoted the exact same transcript references as the Trial Chamber did in support of this statement and that no new evidence was proffered by the Prosecution on appeal concerning this event, we respectfully submit that this is not a contentious issue. It follows, Mr. President, that the Appeals Chamber indeed did not know that Panic heard the conversation, that Mrksic did not, during this conversation, tell Sljivancanin about the withdrawal. Now, that's only the first step. There's a second step to this analysis. Quite simply, if you look at the inference adopted by the Appeals Chamber at paragraph 62, and I read the inference: The only reasonable conclusion that can be drawn is that Mrksic must have told Sljivancanin that he had withdrawn the JNA protection from the prisoners of war out of Ovcara and thus also Sljivancanin's responsibility for the prisoners of war. In drawing this far-reaching inference, it is of the utmost importance to recall, Mr. President, that the Appeals Chamber neither referred to the role of Miodrag Panic during and/or in respect of the Mrksic/Sljivancanin conversation, nor to what he heard of this conversation. We must recall in Celebici the Appeals Chamber found at paragraph 458 that: "If in a case of circumstantial evidence there is a conclusion which is reasonably open from the evidence and which is consistent with the innocence of the accused, he must be acquitted." The Appeals Chamber recently reiterated this finding or this holding in the Boskoski appeals judgement at paragraph 271. It follows, Mr. President, that an inference such as the one that was drawn at paragraph 62 of the appeals judgement can only be drawn if it is the only reasonable conclusion available on the basis of the evidence on the record. The Appeals Chamber knows its own case law and there's no doubt, this is not an appeal. We don't doubt that the Appeals Chamber applied its own case law, but obviously if the Appeals Chamber had known of the new information proffered by Panic during his testimony this morning, that he heard the conversation, and that Mrksic did not tell Sljivancanin about the withdrawal, then the Appeals Chamber would have done one of two things. Either the Appeals Chamber would simply not have drawn the inference that Mrksic must have told Sljivancanin about the order; or, if the Appeals Chamber still decided to draw this inference, while before drawing such a far-reaching inference, I have no doubt that the Appeals Chamber would have explained why the fact that Panic said that he heard the conversation and that Mrksic did not tell Sljivancanin that this was not an obstacle to the Appeals Chamber drawing that inference. So what I'm saying in a nutshell, the fact that the Appeals Chamber neither referred to the role of Panic during the conversation or in respect of the Mrksic/Sljivancanin conversation, nor even to the fact that he heard the conversation, that makes it clear that the evidence proffered this morning by Miodrag Panic was not known to the Appeals Chamber and indeed constitutes a new fact. In this regard, Mr. President, it is interesting to note the Prosecution argument raised at paragraphs 13 and 14 of its response, that the evidence proffered by Panic is not new because Panic said during his testimony that he did not know who issued the order. Now, that's very interesting because it actually supports what I'm telling you today. Now, bearing in mind the testimony of Panic at trial. Firstly, he says I know Sljivancanin spoke to the commander upon his return to the command. That's 14330, line 7. Secondly, Panic says that he did not know who ordered the withdrawal of the MPs from Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Bourgon, as a very talented lawyer for Mr. Sljivancanin, how come during the trial you did not try to question Mr. Panic more closely about the content of the conversation?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Because at the time, Mr. President, it was not a relevant issue. At the time what was of interest to counsel representing Sljivancanin -- now, of course, I was not there but I'm perfectly familiar with the record and able to answer. What was relevant at the time, Mr. President, was whether Sljivancanin was actually present for the daily briefing. And why was this important? Because of the Prosecution's case. The Prosecution's case - and this morning it looked like they were going back to their initial case of a joint criminal enterprise. So it was very important for counsel for the Defence of Sljivancanin to establish that he was not present at the briefing. Why? Because there was evidence coming in because -- during the Prosecution's case that this is where and around the time that the order was given. So to show that he was not part of that joint criminal enterprise, the focus of the Defence case was exactly to show that he was not at the briefing. When Mr. Panic answered that he was not at the briefing, there was no reason to question him further. Had the Prosecution put the case to Sljivancanin when he testified, of course the Defence would have asked Panic, of course it would; but it didn't. Had the Prosecution put the question to Panic: What did you hear? Of course the Defence would have done something about that, but it didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: But what about the 8.00 p.m. meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, the 8.00 p.m. was exactly this, Mr. President, it was Sljivancanin arriving at the command, arriving late at the command. And when he arrived, the briefing was over. That was it. That was the issue that was of importance to the Defence, and the Defence moved on. When Panic testified, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: But the meeting went on and things could have been said during that meeting. Wasn't it natural that you would ask Panic questions about it? Did you hear anything about the order? Didn't you hear anything about the order?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, we're on the Defence side. If somebody must establish something, it's the Prosecution. If the Prosecution had put questions, they have the burden of proof. The Defence does not have any obligation or any need and it would be stupid for the Defence to go into events that it doesn't have the answer. It's a basic line that you never ask a question to which you don't know the answer. I'm sure Mr. Lukic wished that he had asked Mr. Panic about that conversation when he met with him before his testimony. I wish -- I'm sure Mr. Lukic would dream that during the trial that issue would have come out because we wouldn't be here today, but it didn't and we can't be blamed for that. The Defence cannot be blamed for this at all, Mr. President. Thank you. Now, I move on to the thing that -- my argument which was that Panic said: I know Sljivancanin talked to the commander, but I don't know who issued the order for the withdrawal -- I don't know -- no, sorry. He knows that Sljivancanin talked to the commander upon his return to the command. That's 14330, line 7. And secondly, he said that he did not know who ordered the withdrawal of the MPs from Ovcara. Now, if you take these two things together, it follows that if the Appeals Chamber had known or if it had been established that Panic either was a party to the conversation or that he heard the conversation, then the Appeals Chamber could not have drawn the inference without first distancing its from what Panic said, or else the inference could not be the only reasonable conclusion. Consequently, the fact that the Appeals Chamber - now we're looking at what is existing today and not maybes - the Appeals Chamber did not enter into such details. It demonstrates that the Appeals Chamber did not know that Panic heard the conversation and that the Appeals Chamber did not -- certainly did not know that Panic heard that Mrksic did not tell Sljivancanin about the withdrawal. Hence, the argument put forward by the Prosecution actually confirms that the evidence proffered by Panic this morning is indeed a new fact. I have 15 more minutes to go, Mr. President. I move to my third argument, and that is that our submission that another way to consider this, the evidence of Panic, is to look at all previous decisions rendered by the Appeals Chamber of both the ICTY and the ICTR in respect of applications for review. To this day, some 18 applications for review have been filed before the Appeals Chamber. I say some 18 because we -- you well know, Mr. President, there were some mixed applications for review and reconsideration. Some 18 applications. One such application was granted, while all others were denied. I hesitate in saying this, but I have to, Mr. President. I know how difficult these applications are for the Appeals Chamber. I know how important the finality of judgements is. I know that. It's been a long time when I was chef de cabinet in this place, but I do remember, just as Judge Guney, I'm sure, remembers the secretary I gave him when I was chef de cabinet. I remember sitting with the Judges when the Barayagwiza application was granted. I know the debates. I know how it took place. I know how it was done. I know how difficult it is. But when we have exceptional circumstances, it is important, Mr. President, that we take them into consideration. Now, looking at this application, the Barayagwiza application, which was granted, it reads the following: The Appeals Chamber held "a relevant new fact emerges from this" application. "In its Decision, the Chamber determined from the basis of the evidence adduced at the time that 'Cameroon was willing to transfer the accused' as there was no proof to the contrary. The above information, however," the new fact, "goes to show that Cameroon had not been prepared to effect its transfer before 24 October 1997. This fact is new." That's what the Appeals Chamber said at paragraph 57. It is evident that applying this finding to the ICTR Appeals Chamber to the present case, that the evidence of Witness Panic heard this morning is indeed a new fact. The Appeals Chamber adopted the inference at paragraph 62 on the basis that there was no direct evidence that Mrksic told Sljivancanin that he had withdrawn the MPs from Ovcara. The evidence of Witness Panic not only provides direct evidence as to what was said, it also provides evidence that Mrksic did not tell Sljivancanin about the withdrawal during this conversation. Other examples where the Appeals Chamber concluded that the evidence proffered did constitute new facts, even though these applications were later denied for other reasons, can be found in Tadic motion for review, 30 July 2002. The Appeals Chamber said: "Findings of the Appeals Chamber made after the final judgements were considered as new facts." In Josipovic, first motion for review, 7 March 2003, where the discovery of a policeman who resembles Josipovic and who could have been involved in the attack on Ahmici was considered to be a new fact because it was not litigated at trial. In the Rutaganda application for review, 9 December 2006, where findings were made in another case on the general lack of credibility and about the fact that statements given to Rwandan authorities prior to the testimony of some witnesses -- of two material witnesses were considered new facts because they were not in issue at trial. Comparing these three instances to the evidence provided by Panic this morning, which was neither known by the Appeals Chamber nor litigated and/or in issue at trial or on appeal because no questions were put to the relevant witnesses, inter alia, that's one of the reasons, reveals the same conclusion. The information provided by Panic is indeed a new fact. As for the other decisions rendered by the Appeals Chamber, the nine applications for review, the rationale appears to have been quite constant that the proposed evidence constituted additional evidence of the fact in issue, and therefore were not new facts. If we consider the testimony of Witness Panic, we -- it is our respectful submission that it cannot be considered to be additional evidence of a fact in issue. This rationale simply does not apply in the present case. That is why this case not only raises some exceptional circumstances but can be distinguished from all other applications which have been denied. I can move into explaining why the fact was not in issue, but the Trial Chamber's conclusion was that Sljivancanin does not possess the requisite mens rea for aiding and abetting murder as long as he was under the understanding that the JNA troops remained at Ovcara. That's the finding, that's the part that was in issue at trial. Whether Sljivancanin learned that the JNA troops guarding the prisoners at Ovcara were removed, a far-reaching interpretation would say it probably became an issue when the Appeals Chamber put the question to the parties at the end of the appeal, when all briefs were in, and then there were oral arguments. However, considering the findings of the Trial Chamber that Mrksic issued the order to withdraw the MPs from Ovcara, that Sljivancanin was not involved in the transmission of this order, and while it may also be considered on that basis that whether Sljivancanin learned that Mrksic had withdrawn the MPs from Ovcara and if so when, whether that was an issue on appeal because of the question put by the Appeals Chamber, it is significant that this was not the Prosecution's theory and has never been until final oral arguments. Quite to the contrary. The Prosecution's second ground of appeal was the following: "It was unreasonable for the Trial Chamber to find that it was unable to conclude that at the time of its visit to Ovcara Sljivancanin was aware that the prisoners of war would probably be murdered." More importantly, if we look at the evidence adduced by the parties at trial, especially by the Prosecution, it is evident that the issue whether Sljivancanin learned that Mrksic had withdrawn the MPs from Ovcara was not litigated and certainly not disputed by the parties. The only witnesses who said anything about that conversation between Mrksic and Sljivancanin is Sljivancanin himself. And the Prosecution never put the question to him: Did Mrksic inform you or didn't Mrksic tell you, Mr. Sljivancanin? Nothing like that. He was questioned, but not on that issue. All other witnesses who testified at trial and who could have offered any evidence in relation to the issue whether Sljivancanin learned that Mrksic had ordered the withdrawal of the MPs from Ovcara were meant -- never put to any witnesses in this regard. Now, this includes Trifunovic, Gluscevic, Vukasinovic, Sljivancanin, Vojnovic, and Lesanovic, and of course Witness Panic whom we've heard this morning. Consequently, Mr. President, whether and when Sljivancanin learned that Mrksic had withdrawn the MPs from Ovcara were certainly not disputed by the parties at trial and was not disputed on appeal and no new evidence was submitted by the Prosecution on appeal, even though the burden of proof rests on the Prosecution. In these circumstances, the direct evidence by Panic that Mrksic did not inform Sljivancanin that he had withdrawn the MPs from Ovcara can in no way considered to be additional evidence. I move on quickly. I have I think three minutes left. My fourth and last argument, Mr. President. It is our respectful submission that the arguments put forward by the Prosecution in arguing that the evidence by Panic is not a new fact focuses on details, just as my colleague did this morning when cross-examining Witness Panic, but that they missed the most obvious conclusion, which stems from the testimony of Witness Panic and on which the present review application rests. In other words, the Prosecution is asking you to look at the trees while at the same time it is telling you to ignore the forest. On the one hand the acquittal of Sljivancanin was reversed on appeal on the basis of a single watershed inference made in the absence of direct evidence that Mrksic told Sljivancanin about the withdrawal. On the other hand, the evidence proffered by Witness Panic provides a source of direct evidence, while establishing that Mrksic did not tell Sljivancanin about the withdrawal during that conversation. Mr. President, if that doesn't qualify as new fact, then nothing ever well. The purpose of Article 26 applications is precisely to prevent a miscarriage of justice in situations where new information unknown to the deciding body at the time the decision was rendered makes it clear that the decision was erroneous. It is obvious that the evidence offered by Witness Panic is one such situation. Yes, that is the -- the Prosecution is asking you to ignore, the forest. We, on the other hand, take this opportunity to recall the holding of the ICTR Appeals Chamber in the Barayagwiza case which is directly applicable because to reject the fact by Panic in the light of the impact on the decision would indeed be to close one's eyes to reality. A quick, Mr. President, conclusion, simply to say - I had more but I will stop here - simply to say that I raise today four different ways to look at new fact: A case law, the jurisprudence, the plain meaning of the words, and the forest test. You look at any way you want at -- if you try to find that the thing that -- this was an issue at trial, it was not. Any way you look at it, we find that what Panic said this morning is indeed something that is new and that was unknown to the deciding body. I close with one quick sentence, and very quickly because it's not the gist of our application today. But should there be any doubt that it's not a new fact, that it's not a new fact, then we say as two learned Judges have put in separate opinion - yourself, Mr. President, and Judge Shahabuddeen - you still have the power as the Appeals Chamber to make things right. Of course, that's not what we're asking today. But if it's not a new fact - and we are certain that it is a new fact - but even if that is not, you still have the power to make things right and that is very important because you heard the man this morning and that was not told to Sljivancanin in the night of 20 November 1991 and his conviction cannot stand. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon, for your argument. And, Ms. Brady, you're taking over. You have 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Panic's evidence, even if it were to be accepted - which for all the reasons given by my colleague Mr. Rogers this morning it should not be - but even if it were to be accepted by you, it still doesn't meet the test for a new fact which is required to trigger a review by the Appeals Chamber of its judgement. And for this reason, Sljivancanin's application must be dismissed. Based on consistent ICTY and ICTR Appeals Chamber jurisprudence, his testimony that we heard today does not amount to a new fact. During both the trial and the appeal, the issue of what Sljivancanin -- excuse me, whether Sljivancanin learnt of the withdrawal of the 80th Motorised Brigade from Ovcara; who he learnt it from, that is, Mrksic; when he learnt it, that is, at 2000 hours on the 20th of November; where he learnt it, that is, at the command post; and how he learnt it, that is, in that meeting, was litigated and considered. Sljivancanin testified about these matters, and we disagree with Mr. Bourgon's point about this in the -- that he's just made. We disagree with him when he says it's not additional evidence of those facts; in fact, Panic's testimony that we've heard today is simply additional evidence of the facts that were previously litigated and considered. And on the case law, this is insufficient to trigger a review. Your Honours, in the case law on review proceedings, the Appeals Chamber has carefully distinguished between on the one hand a fact -- a new fact, and on the other hand what is additional evidence of a fact which has already been litigated or considered by the original deciding Chamber. And the Appeals Chamber has defined a new fact as this, and I'm quoting: "Information of an evidentiary nature supporting a fact that was not in issue during the trial or appeal proceedings. The requirement that the fact was not in issue during the proceedings means that it must not have been among the factors that the deciding body could have taken into account in reaching its verdict." And as we know, only a showing of a new fact will open the door to review proceedings. As you've emphasized, this Chamber's emphasized in the Delic review decision, where the additional material proffered consists of a new fact, that is, a fact which was not in issue or considered in the original proceedings, a review pursuant to Rule 119 is the appropriate procedure which must be taken before the Chamber which gave the final judgement upon the relevant issue. "If the material proffered consists of additional evidence relating to a fact which was in issue or considered in the original proceedings, this does not constitute a new fact within the meaning of Rule 119 and the review procedure is not available." And as I'll develop during the course of my submissions this afternoon, the Appeals Chamber's approach that it has taken to defining a new fact reflects the exceptional nature of the review proceeding, and in particular the interest in finality and certainty of judgements. Now, coming right to the point of what is the new fact. The applicant, Mr. Sljivancanin, says that this new fact coming -- emanating from Panic's testimony is that Panic, who was present during the conversation between Mrksic and Sljivancanin on the night of the 20th of November, that he heard the conversation, but he did not hear Mrksic tell Sljivancanin that he had ordered the withdrawal of the 80th Motorised Brigade from Ovcara. Having framed the alleged new fact in this very specific way, this very narrow way, he then looks back at the trial and the appeal proceedings and he argues that this specific piece of evidence -- in fact, we heard in his submissions a number of times, he's always referring -- most frequently referring it as evidence. This specific piece of evidence was not considered or taken into account by the Trial Chamber or the Appeals Chamber in reaching its decision. In our submission, this approach is flawed. If you look at the 20 or so review cases that have previously been considered by this Chamber, what is necessary is to first identify correctly the facts that were in issue in the original proceedings. And having done this, the new information has to be then assessed to see if it can be deemed indeed a new fact or whether it's simply additional evidence of a fact already litigated or considered by the deciding Chamber. And in our submission, applying the proper approach to this case, what Sljivancanin learnt once he returned to the command post at Negoslavci at 2000 hours on the relevant evening, in particular whether he learnt that Mile Mrksic had withdrawn the remaining JNA troops from Ovcara was a fact in issue in both the trial and the appeal proceedings. And I'll start first with the appeal proceedings, since that's the stage in which the factual finding was made. It's not correct -- it's not true to say, as Mr. Bourgon has, that the issue didn't crystallise until the questions were put by the Appeals Chamber. In fact, the Prosecution first raised the issue on appeal in a substantive way in its Prosecution appeal brief filed in January 2008. And, Your Honours, I'll briefly read just two paragraphs from that brief to remind yourselves of our position on this. Paragraph 76 of the Prosecution appeal brief we argued this: "Later that night at approximately 2000 hours Sljivancanin learned more about the events at Ovcara, including that Mrksic had ordered the JNA to withdraw." Then at paragraph 102 we elaborated further: "Sljivancanin returned to Negoslavci at approximately 2000 hours on the 20th of November, 1991, and was briefed on events at Ovcara by Major Vukasinovic. He then reported to Mrksic. The only inference available on this evidence was that Sljivancanin was informed of Mrksic's order upon his return to Negoslavci. Sljivancanin admitted that he had a conversation about the transfer of the prisoners when he returned to Negoslavci that night." And the footnote for that is a reference to Sljivancanin's testimony about this meeting that he had with Mrksic when he returned to the command post. Now, the Trial Chamber hadn't made an affirmative finding on this issue of whether he learnt and how he learnt it. If you look at the trial judgement paragraph 389 and 661, they didn't make an affirmative or positive finding in favour of the Prosecution on that point. So it was an important point to establish, a finding on this issue had to be made by the Appeals Chamber in order to trigger Sljivancanin's duty to protect the prisoners. And the factual finding at issue -- it's clear from what I've read, the factual finding at issue concerned Sljivancanin's conversation with Mrksic that evening at the command post. And the Defence answered in some detail in his response brief several paragraphs were dedicated to this issue, paragraphs 178 to 179 and 208 to 216. Sljivancanin not only denied being aware that Mrksic had issued an order to withdraw the JNA from Ovcara, but he specifically argued that: "The evidence as well as the conclusions of the Trial Chamber do not show that Mrksic informed Sljivancanin that he had ordered the JNA security to be withdrawn from Ovcara on 20 November 1991." So this issue, what Sljivancanin learned that evening, and his conversation with Mrksic in particular, was a factual issue for determination in the appeal. And the parties clearly saw it that way. The Appeals Chamber recognised this in its addendum to the Scheduling Order, which came out a couple of weeks I think before the appeals hearing. It focused on -- the Chamber focused on Sljivancanin's claim that he didn't know that Mrksic ordered the withdrawal, and the parties were asked to elaborate on this issue, this very factual issue, when Sljivancanin learned of Mrksic's order to withdraw the JNA troops. And the parties gave extensive answers on this issue at the appeals hearing. That's at transcripts pages 219 to 224 for the Prosecution's submissions on this point and 283 to 287 for the Defence submissions. And we advocated that the only reasonable conclusion was that when he returned to the command post that night at that time, 2000 hours, that he must have learnt of the withdrawal order and pointing in particular to his conversation with Mrksic and its content. And I recall reading large chunks -- quotes of Sljivancanin's testimony, direct evidence about this conversation. And the Appeals Chamber itself then devoted the majority -- devoted two lengthy paragraphs on this issue to what Sljivancanin found out when he returned to the command post. It looked at -- the Chamber must have looked at the totality of the evidence in the trial record, including Sljivancanin's testimony about his conversation with Mrksic, amongst which topics they discussed with the facts that the prisoners were at Ovcara and were now under the authority of the SAO government. The relevant parts of Sljivancanin's testimony being 13665 and 13983 to 13988. And from this, the Appeals Chamber made its critical finding in paragraph 62 that Mrksic must have told Sljivancanin he had withdrawn the troops from Ovcara. Now, before I move on to speak about the issue -- this factual issue being litigated at trial, I do want to make one comment about Mr. Bourgon's submissions on the changes in the translation from B/C/S into English. In our submission, none of the changes that were made that were approved by the CLSS from the B/C/S into English about that conversation affect the import of the conversation. But there is one point I do wish to correct because Mr. Bourgon indicated that the testimony of Sljivancanin had been corrected -- this is Sljivancanin's testimony at 13665. He said that it had been corrected in -- if I understand correctly in two points. And we agree with the first point but not with the second. It's true that the translation has been corrected so that it now says that Sljivancanin called in on Colonel Mrksic instead of using the word I think "reported." But Mr. Bourgon also mentioned that the change was made by CLSS so that it now reads "I briefly informed him on what was basically happening with the hospital." But in fact, Your Honours, that change was not accepted by CLSS. CLSS in fact kept the original wording "I briefly informed them," and relevant as well to this point is that if you take a look at a further part of Sljivancanin's evidence - and this is when he's under cross-examination at 13983 - in fact, under cross-examination Sljivancanin again gives his version of the conversation or part of it and he says at paragraph -- at page 13983, line -- well, I'll start at line 18, Sljivancanin answers: "I went to see Mrksic to tell him what I'd seen at the hospital and what happened at the hospital that day and to see what would be further tasks and duties." And then dropping down to line 22 he says this: "And since the Chief of Staff, Mr. Panic, was there, I believed them to be in the know, in the sense of knowing exactly what was going on, why those people had gone there." Which does tend to support the version of CLSS, that he originally briefed them. Your Honours, the issue of Sljivancanin's knowledge that night when he returned to the command post and his conversation with Mrksic was also a factual issue at trial. I've spoken already about the appeal stage, but the Appeals Chamber clearly made its findings on the basis of evidence and factual findings of the Trial Chamber. Now, the fact that the Prosecution's case at trial was more extensive -- because at trial the Prosecution alleged that Sljivancanin was part of a joint criminal enterprise to harm and to kill the prisoners, and also we alleged that he had himself been involved in the transmittal of the order, of the withdrawal order, but that fact does not mean, as he argues or he argued today, that what he learnt, what Sljivancanin learnt when he returned to Negoslavci and his conversation with Mrksic were not facts in issue. And allow me to explain what I mean. To the contrary, what Sljivancanin did and what he knew in the evening when he got back were relevant, both to a proper consideration of his earlier conduct, whether it was part of the Prosecution's theory on joint criminal enterprise or not, what he found out later was still relevant to a proper consideration of his earlier conduct and to his Defence of those matters. And no doubt that's part of the reason -- one of the reasons why Sljivancanin's counsel actually asked Sljivancanin about his meeting with Mrksic. Let's -- we recall that the conversation that Sljivancanin had with Mrksic was first raised by a question in examination-in-chief. And the tenor of the question and the answer shows that it was being done to show that Sljivancanin when he got back to the command post that night, it was more or less business as usual, he was asking for his next tasks and duties, and he didn't get any information. He continued to remain uninformed about the fate of the prisoners. That is more or less the purpose of this line of questioning. Indeed, his evidence -- his state of mind after the events has always -- has been an even more longer-term issue. His evidence at trial was that he remained ignorant of the fate of the prisoners until many years later, something like 1998 when he actually found out, he says, for sure about what happened to the prisoners. He heard rumours swirling around, but he says he didn't know for sure until he called to the military proceedings in Belgrade in 1998. So what he knew and what he found out always was a very relevant issue for him both in meeting the Prosecution's case and in running his defence. What's also interesting to note is that at trial Sljivancanin also had to deal with or meet Mrksic's defence. Now, Mrksic's defence -- now, Mrksic's defence was not accepted by the Trial Chamber or the Appeals Chamber, but it's relevant to an understanding of what were the facts in issue at the trial. Because Mrksic's defence was that sometime between 7.00 to 8.00 that night he left Negoslavci on a helicopter and went to Belgrade and leaving his Chief of Staff, deputy commander Panic, in charge. And Mrksic's argument - again, it wasn't accepted - but his argument was that the order to withdraw happened on Panic's watch, and he pointed to the security administration as the likely source. So again, what Sljivancanin knew, his interactions and his discussions with Mrksic that evening, were facts in issue -- facts in issue, given this attempt by Mrksic to shift the blame to Panic and the security administration, and thereby also by implication to Sljivancanin. In fact, when cross-examined by Mrksic's counsel about the timing of his conversation with Mrksic that evening, and in particular Sljivancanin's claim that Mrksic had told him that the government had taken over the -- a group of suspects, Sljivancanin said this under cross-examination by Mr. Vasic, this is at transcript 13724 to 725: "... I know not 100 per cent, but with 1 million per cent certainty that I was at the commander's on the 20th, in the evening. As for the government session, before hearing about it from the commander, I heard it from my security officer, Srecko Borisavljevic." So for Sljivancanin to now say that the issue of what he found out that evening about the prisoners and in particular their loss of protection, the withdrawal of the security detail, was not a live issue during the trial proceedings is baseless. The Trial Chamber didn't make an affirmative finding as to whether Sljivancanin learnt about the withdrawal order that evening, didn't make a positive finding on that issue, but this doesn't mean as Sljivancanin alleges that somehow it didn't consider the matter. If you look at the clear wording of paragraphs 389 and 661, it shows that the Trial Chamber did consider the issue but they weren't sufficiently persuaded by the evidence to make a finding. And that's exactly why we asked Your Honours on appeal to make this finding because the Trial Chamber had not made a finding in favour of the Prosecution. So in a nutshell, Your Honours, those are the previously litigated facts: What he learnt, the withdrawal of the 80th from Ovcara; who he learnt it from, Mrksic; when he learnt it, at 2000 hours on the 20th of November, 1991; where he learnt it, at the command post; and how he learnt it, in that meeting. If we now turn to examine Panic's recent evidence, recent testimony that we heard this morning and compare it to these facts which were already litigated and considered, it is simply additional evidence pertaining to these already-litigated facts. And in fact several times in his written submissions the applicant has said it's evidence corroborating Sljivancanin's evidence at trial. Now, the gist of his argument today is that neither the Appeals Chamber or the Trial Chamber had before it this specific piece of evidence that Panic now provides, that Panic did not hear Mrksic tell Sljivancanin that he had ordered the security detail to be withdrawn. There are two answers to this. Firstly, even if you were to take a more elastic approach to the concept of a new fact in this case, even if you were to adopt the approach being advocated by Mr. -- by Mr. Sljivancanin and his team, this evidence was already before the Trial Chamber and the Appeals Chamber. You have to consider two different factors in this: Firstly, both Sljivancanin and Panic testified at trial that Panic was present when Sljivancanin met with Mrksic that evening. Mr. Rogers this morning read to you Panic's evidence at transcript 14330, just to remind you what he said. Panic's -- Panic was asked whether Sljivancanin attended the 6.00 p.m. briefing: "Do you have any memory of that" and "did you see him that evening at all." And after going through the -- that he doesn't remember seeing him at the briefing, Panic then says that: "I think he came," he being Sljivancanin, "I think he came, say, around 2000 hours and I know that he talked to the commander." So there's no issue; he's there. Now, Panic testified at trial that he never knew who ordered the withdrawal. His position is he never knew who ordered the withdrawal, but basically over time he has some to accept or to conclude, reluctantly or otherwise, that it must have come from Mrksic. And I invite Your Honours to read carefully Panic's testimony at pages 14409 to 10 and 14498 to 502. I will briefly go into this testimony to make this point. At transcript page 14409 Mr. Panic was asked this: "Q. Well, who was tasked with handing over those people to the civilian authorities? "A. Well, that's the problem, that's the issue that has to be proved. "Q. Do you know this? "A. No, I don't. But when this becomes evident, then the truth will be known about these events. There was supposed to be no hand-over to anyone by our command. They were supposed to be screened, selected. The combatants were supposed to be separated off from the non-combatants, the patients, and the wounded, and they were to be transported to Sremska Mitrovica. Nowhere was anything said by anyone in anyone's presence at the command post, in the barracks, or anywhere else in the area at that time about their handing over to the civilian authorities. The problem of who handed them over is something that has to be proved, and when this is proved it will be easier to arrive at the truth about this case." So here he is saying no one ever said anything, including at the command post. And he knows -- at trial, he knows this is the crux of the issue in the case. He in fact again this morning referred to this as the crux of the matter. I also take you to his -- a later part of his evidence at 14498 [sic] to -- this is Panic under cross-examination by the Prosecution, where he reluctantly concludes that the order must have come from Mrksic. It was a bit surprising today to hear his submissions that he was so surprised when he read the appeal judgement because, in fact, at trial he had more or less reached the conclusion that Mrksic must have ordered it. But nevertheless, you can make that -- make of that what you will. But at page 14498, the Prosecution is putting to Panic his previous OTP statement and in particular paragraph 92 of that OTP statement. And he reads it to -- Mr. Weiner, the Prosecution trial attorney reads it to Panic. Question -- he quotes from paragraph 92 of the OTP statement: "Q. 'In my opinion, the two central issues concerning Ovcara are: One, how long the JNA can secure the hangar. Two, why did the JNA leave the area. The order for the withdrawal of the military police could have been issued only by the commander of the military police of either the Guards Motorised Brigade or the 80th Motorised Brigade. As the commander of OG South, Colonel Mile Mrksic was the highest-ranking commander in the area. This means the order of the JNA withdrawal must have been issued or at least authorised by him. I know Mrksic very well and cannot imagine he would have issued such an order. However, the order for withdrawal of military police could have only come from him. The military police of the 80th Motorised Brigade withdrew on JNA orders. They were not forced out by the local Serbian TO. Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic could have issued the order for the withdrawal of the military police but not without consulting Mrksic. It is possible that someone carried out the withdrawal of the military police of the 80th Motorised Brigade without'" his "'authorisation, but that would represent a violation of the regulations.'" He's asked: "Is that what you said, sir?" And he answers: "Yes." And then for the next four or so pages Panic agrees with each of the propositions in greater detail in that statement. So from these facts, the facts that he was present and the facts that he never knew that Mrksic had given the order to withdraw. These in fact established at trial Panic's denial of having heard Mrksic tell Sljivancanin on the evening or, indeed, ever that he had ordered the withdrawal of the 80th from Ovcara. Now, it's true that Panic never affirmatively said at trial the words -- he never said in his testimony: I did not hear Mrksic tell Sljivancanin he had ordered the withdrawal of the security detail at Ovcara. But in fact it's the only logical implication of his and Sljivancanin's trial evidence. So that's addressing the evidence put forward in the interpretation of new facts that Mr. Bourgon would give to it. We say that that is actually too narrow, but even if you take that narrow approach this matter was already before you and before the Trial Chamber. But secondly, and the more correct approach, is that Panic adds nothing more to what Sljivancanin already testified about at trial. What he offers is simply additional evidence of a fact which has been previously litigated and considered. This fact, which I've stressed throughout the submissions, what Sljivancanin learned, when he learnt it, where he learnt it, who he learnt it from, and how he learnt it. The who, what, when, where, how that I've been speaking about this afternoon. And this testimony that we heard today from Mr. Panic is no different from the additional evidence which this Appeals Chamber has rejected as a new fact in a host of previous review cases. And I think we take quite a different view of the case law from that which has been put forward by the applicant this afternoon. In fact, the overwhelming majority of cases on this new fact support the Prosecution position. I won't go through all those cases, but, for example, the Appeals Chamber has rejected as a new fact new evidence which was put forward to establish an alibi which had already been -- which had been presented at trial. This is in the Josipovic 7 March 2003 case, the Niyitegeka case or cases. And the reason that the Appeals Chamber gave is that because the issue of alibi was previously litigated and considered at trial. The Appeals Chamber has also rejected as a new fact new evidence which tended to show that a witness relied upon by the Trial Chamber for a factual -- for a conviction was not credible. This is in the Naletilic decision 19 March 2009 and the Niyitegeka case 12 March 2007. Why? Why did it reject it? Because the issue of the credibility of the witness had already been considered at trial. Likewise, Your Honours have rejected as a new fact or rejected classifying as a new fact evidence which was put forward which tended to undermine the identity of the accused as the assailant of the crime. This is in the Delic case, 25 April 2002. Again, if you look at the reasoning, why was this? The Appeals Chamber said this is because the identity of the accused as the person who took the victim out and beat him had already been discussed and considered at trial. Likewise, in the Radic case, 31 October 2006, this Chamber rejected as a new fact new evidence which showed the accused had no access to a room in which he had been found to have raped a victim. And the reasoning was that the issue of accessibility and use of the room by the accused had already been considered at trial. And finally, Your Honours, you've rejected as a new fact in a Prosecution application in the Blaskic case 23 November 2006, where you rejected as a new fact new evidence showing that oral orders may have been given by the accused, again, on the basis of the issue of whether the accused ordered the crimes in Ahmici had already been considered at trial, albeit in the form of written orders. Panic's evidence is no different from any of these cases in which the Appeals Chamber rejected classifying the new information as a new fact. And, in our submission, following these precedents, you should likewise reject his testimony today as being a new fact sufficient to trigger a review. Your Honours, I won't address the other criteria for review, the second and third criteria have been amply dealt with in our response brief, as has the fourth criteria for review. We stand by our submissions in the response brief. In my conclusion, I would like to reiterate a couple of points made by Mr. Rogers this morning about Panic's evidence. Panic's evidence is not credible, it's not reasonably capable of belief; in our submission, it's manufactured as a memory. It's offered 18 years after the events to continue to try and distance himself and Sljivancanin from any responsibility whatsoever for what happened to the prisoners at Ovcara. I also just will briefly respond to a point made by Mr. Bourgon this afternoon, where he said he was surprised that the Prosecution had asked this Chamber to apply specific findings on credibility by the Trial Chamber and to apply this question -- apply this reasoning to questions which were never put to Panic. Perhaps I have missed his point, but he seems to miss ours. Our point is that the same fundamental credibility analysis applied by the Trial Chamber should apply here today. I mean, firstly, Your Honours, you have upheld the Trial Chamber's credibility findings about Panic. But secondly, it -- the same reasoning applied by the Trial Chamber applies to your consideration of his evidence today because, put quite simply, when Panic gets to matters that could implicate him or expose him or somehow not present his role in the favourable way that he wishes it to be shown, he is - I think Mr. Rogers put it quite well this morning - he is economical with the truth. In fact, we could say that he is not credible and that he greatly underplays his role, his knowledge, what he knew, and what he saw, what he heard. And this is yet just another example, what we heard this morning, of his distancing himself from anything that could touch him or hurt him or increase his responsibility in any way. But, Your Honours, even if you were to find Mr. Panic's evidence credible, no matter how broadly or narrowly you characterise the facts previously in issue, whether you characterise them as what Sljivancanin learnt that evening about the troop withdrawal, whether you characterise it as Sljivancanin's conversation with Mrksic, even if you characterise it on the more narrow basis that the applicant would -- how the applicant would frame the issue, that Panic did not hear Mrksic tell Sljivancanin he had ordered the JNA withdrawal, no matter how you characterise the old facts versus the new facts, you will not find that Panic's testimony amounts to a new fact; it simply fails to meet the test. Your Honours, that concludes my submissions this afternoon, and I'd be happy to answer any questions if Your Honours have any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Brady. I see there are no questions. So on to you for the last 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'll try to be even shorter than 15 minutes. The first issue I'd like to respond to is what my colleague from the Prosecution said concerning the memorandum we received from CLSS about the translation issue. Translation initially came back from CLSS. On the first issue they say "I tell," "I wanted to tell," without the "them." They agree, we agree. On the second issue it came back and the "them" was still there. We listened to the tape again, we returned that to CLSS saying there's a problem because in our understanding the "them" is not there. It came back to us saying, Well, the issue is the verb "inform" requires an object, so it has to be "him" or "them." Now, if you read that paragraph and that paragraph was like this, the exact paragraph was: "I briefly informed them on what was basically happening with the hospital ..." But if you read the complete paragraph to which this applies, "this is what I called in on Mrksic," so it can't be "I called in on Mrksic and I briefed them." It must be "I called in on Mrksic and I informed him." You know, to be logical in the same paragraph he can't talk about one man and then say "them." The object is there but the object must have been "him." That's, of course, that's our submission, which can always be checked. The second issue I'd like to address, Mr. President, is my colleague said that whether or not there was a JCE argument at the beginning makes no difference, a joint criminal enterprise argument. Well, Mr. President, we say it does make a difference in terms of what the questions -- what questions are put to the witnesses and what evidence is led by the Prosecution. And in order to get their joint criminal enterprise case that they were looking for, they were interested in ensuring that Sljivancanin was part of the process and that he was involved in the transmission of the order. And of course, as we all know, they failed in their argument and the Trial Chamber said there is no joint criminal enterprise and there was no involvement of Sljivancanin regarding -- regarding the transmission of the order. If there was an issue at trial, that was it. The issue of Sljivancanin's knowledge of the withdrawal itself were certainly not in issue at trial and we did that in our briefs already. The issue is did it become an issue on appeal? And we say absolutely not. If it had been an issue on appeal, Mr. President, the Prosecution would have made it a ground of appeal. They would not have said the Trial Chamber erred by saying that Sljivancanin erred in saying that he did not get the mens rea in the afternoon when he was at Ovcara. They would say the Trial Chamber erred because they failed to see that Mrksic informed him and that he gained the mens rea at night. That's not at all what they said. They may have said in their argument that at 8.00 at the command post he learned more, his knowledge became greater, that did not make it an issue. The next point I want to raise, Mr. President, is, you know, the Prosecution today, they keep insisting on the notion of issue. Of course, there's nothing more confusing than trying to find out what is an issue. Is it a fact in issue, is it a material fact, is it a key fact? That's not the point. The point here is did the deciding body knew the information? We haven't heard much about that today, but one thing we did hear, the Prosecution said, that's already on the record. That's a surprise to me. If it had been on the record, when the Appeals Chamber put the question to the Prosecution: When did Mrksic learn of the order -- when did Sljivancanin learn of the order issued by Mrksic? How come they never said any of that when they responded to the question of the Appeals Chamber? They never said nothing -- they never said: That's already on the record that Panic said about this -- nothing like that was mentioned by the Prosecution. Now, I can guess why, but that's not the point. The same applies to us. As the respondent, did we refer to that information on the record? Of course we didn't. Is there any doubt in anyone's mind in this room that if we had known what Panic said this morning that we would not have used that when we responded to your question on appeal? That says it all, Mr. President. It's completely new. We would have said -- we would have told you: Listen, Mr. President, we have this witness. We would have talked about Panic. We're the respondent. And we didn't. That says it all. Last thing is if it was an issue, as they say, how come they didn't raise the question? They didn't explain that today. How come they did not put the question to Sljivancanin? How come they did not put the question to Panic? How come they did not put the question to anybody? When you look at the case law, when you look at the definitions, when you look at what is important today in order for a review application, you can only come to one conclusion, Mr. President, the evidence we heard this morning is a new fact. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This hearing, this evidentiary hearing, is now over. I would like first of all to say to Mr. Panic, whom I thank, we thank, can now return home. He need not stay in The Hague any longer. And I would like to thank the Registry, the interpreters, of course, but also the parties for their arguments today, and for more or less adhering to the time-line, and the hearing is now over. We will issue our decision when we are ready. Thank you very much.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.03 p.m.
